speechtext:
Mr. LEWIS moved for leave to introduce a Bill (No. 129) respecting Baggage Smashing. He said: This Bill deals with a grievance affecting a great number of people in Canada. I find by statistics in the library, that the number of passengers carried in the year 1910 by the railways, was 35,894,575; and that the freight carried during that time was 74,000,000 tons. According to the computation I have made, there would be about 5,000,000 tons of baggage carried. I wish to state, and I believe it is a fact, that there is more damage done by the railways in. carrying that 5,000,000 tons of baggage, than is done in carrying that 74,000,000 tons of freight. A number of cases have happened in my own experience and others have been related to me. where people prefer to pay freight on their valuable trunks and baggage, and to send them as freight, instead of risking the damage that would happen to them in transit as baggage. The cause of the trouble i3 either the carelessness of the employees in handling the baggage or want of sufficient men. Since the Canadian people have attained to such a degree of comfort and affluence, they delight in their personal belongings, and they carry many valuable articles in their baggage; but very few will allow a small piece of baggage, a valise or suit case, to be taken into the baggage car. Consequently, people who travel, are under the discomfort of tumbling over trunks and valises in the car. If a person has a valuable trunk worth $50, the chances are that in travelling from Ottawa to Toronto, he may suffer damages to that trunk to the extent of $25. The object of my Bill is not to- impose penalties, it is more as a detriment. I will read the Bill:
1 This Act may be cited as The Baggage Smashing Act.
2. Every one is guilty of an offence and liable, on summary conviction before a magistrate, stipendiary magistrate or any one justice of the peace having the power to do alone

such acts as are usually required to he done by two or more justices, to a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars over and above the value of the baggage destroyed or damaged or to one month's imprisonment with or without hard labour, or to both, who wilfully or through negligence destroys or damages any trunk, valise, satchel, box or other baggage when handling such baggage for transportation by railway, vessel, vehicle or any other means of conveyance used by common carriers.
3.	When the person found guilty of a violation of the provisions of section 2 of this Act is an employee of any corporation or company, the magistrate, stipendiary magistrate or justice, may convict such corporation or company of the offence and find it liable for the actual damages caused; the employee, in such case, being held liable only for the penalty.
4 This Act shall come into force by proclamation of the Governor in Council.
Now it is a well, known fact that those who have travelled in the old land are aware that no such trouble occurs, the baggage is handled properly. This baggage smashing, which is the term now used in this country, may be of some benefit to the large manufacturing concerns, who make the trunks, and may help ito make more millionaires in Canada. But I stand here on behalf of the plain people who travel, and who want this thing to be put a stop to. I ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), to look into this-matter, and if this Bill does not cover the point, I hope he will himself, take hold of the difficulty, and see that baggage smashing is put an end to, at present the only remedy is by civil action, ordinary citizens cannot afford law suits with corporations.
I would ask the Minister of Railways, if there is not a law on the Railway Act that covers this 'very thing.

The Railway Act makes the railway company liable for damage to baggage to any amount they carry. My hon. friend speaks of handling baggage in the old land. As a matter of fact, most of that is carried in the railway compartment, because when they send it as baggage, they have to pay for it, while in Canada, a certain amount is carried free. Some of us have noticed that when Englishmen are travelling in. Canada, they have a habit of carrying nearly all their baggage in the trains with them. I am afraid if we were to follow their example, instead of having fewer valises in the aisles of the cars, we would have more. However, I have no objection to the first reading of the Bill. As the members of the House are now not allowed any more trunks, those of us who travel hereafter, will probably carry handbags.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

I move that on Tuesday next the House do go into Committee of the Whole to consider the following proposed resolution. His Excellency has been apprised of the subject matter of this resolution, and has given his assent to it.
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Fisheries Act, chapter 45 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, be amended by enacting that in the province of British Columbia no one shall engage in the manufacture of oil or other commercial products from sea lions, hair seals, sharks or dogfish, nor operate a salmon cannery or sallmon curing establishment, except under license from the minister; that the site of reduction works must be approved by the minister; that operations must proceed within one year from issue of the license for which annual fees shall be required; that the annual fee for a lobster fishing license be increased and based on the total number of pounds of canned lobsters; that the annual returns to the minister by the owner or manager of a lobster factory, through the inspector of fisheries of the district, shall furnish more details and be submitted not later than the 31st day of May, each year, and penalties for failure to make such returns shall be imposed; and that licenses must be obtained for maintaining lobster pounds, with an annual fee for the same.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. C. ETHIER (Two Mountains).
speechtext:
(Translation). Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I rise to a question of privilege which is of concern to myself as a member of this House, but which is also, I believe, of concern to the House as a whole.
For over eight years I have had the honour of being chairman of the Committee on Private Bills. On the 23rd February instant, my action as chairman of that committee was made the occasion of some unfair, misleading and uncalled for criticisms. Reference was made to the stand taken by me at a meeting of the said committee,
on April 22, 1909, and remarks purporting
to have been made by me were quoted and put in print. I wish to contradict these statements, and am anxious to apprise the House of their utter lack of foundation.
The statements to which I take exception were made in a manner which I might term incongruous and unworthy of the position occupied by the person who uttered them. I i-efer to Senator Kirehhoffer, chairman of the Divorce Committee of the Senate, who has thought fit to make the following public statement:
The Divorce Committee of the Senate has been often accused by a member of the House of Commons, named Ethier, who is, or used to be the chairman of the Private Bills Committee in that House, of granting divorces on evidence

If I wished to give him a Roland for his Oliver, I might refer to the honourable senator as ' the man named Kirehhoffer,' but I prefer acting in a more courteous and proper way. Then he continues:
-on evidence you would not hang a cat upon. I think that is the favourite expression used ... Of course, the reporter is anxious to announce that Mr. Ethier, in the Commons, and the Hon. Mr. Cloran, in the Senate, make the above remarks-I mean those original remarks about the hanging of a cat on the evidence; but you are entirely mistaken, because you will find thousands of people believe anything they see in the paper, no matter how thick the head or slimy the tongue that gives utterance to it.
There can be no mistake as to whom he is aiming at, for a little further on, he says:
I shall allude to him as the member for Two Mountains.
And again;
Mr. Ethier made use of the very remark which he quoted. I have no doubt he originated it. I think he is deserving of a great deal of censure.
I humbly submit, Mr. Speaker, that this statement, as I have already stated, is false, uncalled for and without foundation. I never uttered such words neither in 1909 or any other time, and I may quote, for the information of the honourable senator, who may judge for himself, the report which the organ of his own party, the Ottawa ' Citizen,' published of what I said in reference to those relief Bills which are sent down to the Committee on Private Bills after going through the Senate. That paper published the following on April 23rd, 1909:
The matter in which the Senate has been granting divorces this session caused some very pointed remarks by Chairman Ethier in the Private Bills Committee of Commons yesterday morning. The Bill called was that divorcing Mildred G. Wendolyn Patterson, now of Toronto, from Charles Colebrooke Patterson, of Ottawa. ' We have 21 of these

relief Bills from tlie Senate this session, said Mr. Ethier ;	* I think the situation is
most serious, most unusual. For six years I have presided over this committee and for thirteen years been a member of it, and while we are accustomed to have half a dozen each session, the limit is reached this time. I think it amounts to an abuse. I do not want to criticise the action of the Senate, but I cannot escape from the idea that this is going too far. In the different provinces we have laws regarding, separation and even in them the judges are very careful. In these cases we have asked to authorize absolute divorce. Those of us who are fathers of families, should think of the great social evil that is involved and not do in this country as they do in the States. The committee should assert its right to see if the proof given in the Senate is proper. I have looked over the evidence in several cases and do not hesitate to say that it does not justify the report save as to separation. The Senate is granting divorces in cases where a court would not give separation. If you prove a man is a drunkard or a gambler, it is not sufficient to justify divorce. I am not speaking as a Catholic, but on the general principles involved in these cases.'
As will be observed, that was far from asserting that the Senate granted relief on evidence insufficient to hang a cat upon.
Let the hon. senator read the article and he will be satisfied, through the testimony of his own organ, that the charge he made against me with the object of inducing the Senate to censure me, is false and that his statements regarding me on that occasion were without foundation; that he showed undue haste and spoke before securing the requisite information. The ' Citizen's ' report, which I have just quoted, is a truthful account of what I said on April 22nd, 1909.
In vesterday's number of that same paper, I notice an account of what that hon. gentleman stated in his report to the House; it is as follows:
On moving the adoption of the committee report in the Eobertson divorce case, Senator Kirchhofier sketched the history of divorce in Canada. He said the committee has been criticised by Senator Cloran and Mr. Ethier, M.P., and it has been declared that divorces were granted on evidence insufficient to ' bang a cat.'
That is another erroneous statement emanating from the hon. senator. Instead of attempting to induce the Senate to censure a member of the House of Commons, who is unable to vindicate himself on the floor of the Senate, why does he not, if he thinks I should be censured, read the words uttered by the hon. leader hf the opposition when a Bill was introduced for the relief of John Denison Smith, on May 10th, 1909, page 6070, volume 4, of ' Hansard? '

The Chairman of the Committee on Private Bills, I believe, called attention in connection with one of these Mr. ETHIER.
Bills, to a tendency towards acting on evidence of a more or less loose character in considering these Bills for divorce. I have already taken occasion of informing him privately that I entirely concur with the view he expressed.
So the hon. senator should in all fairness
censure the leader of the opposition who held views similar to those given expression by me before the Committee on Private Bills. The hon. leader of the opposition goes on:
Every one who is familiar with the proceedings in courts with regard to such matters is aware that there are some precautions observed in court which do not seem to have received very much attention in the proceedings of the Senate.
At the same sitting of the House, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) stated in answer to the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean):
I have had some experience in connection with divorce courts in the province of New Brunswick and have read the reports of the Divorce Committee in the Senate. In the latter it seems to me divorces have been granted on evidence which would he laughed at in any ordinary court.
*******
I have read the reports and have seen oases in which the question was never even asked as to whether there was any collusion between the parties, and divorces have been granted in eases which were the absolute result of collusion. That would he impossible in proceedings before an ordinary court such as we have in our province.
Here is another hon. member which that hon. senator should get the Senate to censure. I may mention another one.
The hon. member when rising to a question of privilege may refer only to what concerns himself and not to any matter in connection with other hon. members.

I was about to close, Mr. Speaker, but before resuming my seat I was anxious to quote the opinion of the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller). However, I shall abide by your decision.
In conclusion, I submit to the House that no senator should be allowed to cast aspersions, in the way Senator Kirchhofier has done, on a member of the House of Commons whose work is carried on in conjunction with that of the Senate, and I think the language he used should be condemned. I repudiate all he said. I repudiate the uncalled for statements which he made to the effect that I had censured the Senate; never have I done so, as he stated at the sitting of February 23rd instant.
On the orders of the day being called :

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of

Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) whether or not the contract for the construction of the Quebec bridge has been let and, if not, how soon is it expect.ed that will be accomplished. I would like to ask whether there is any truth in the rumour that the chairman of the Quebec Bridge Commission has resigned, and, if so, what is the cause of his resignation?

The contract for the Quebec bridge has not yet been let. The chief engineer has resigned. For a year or more he has intimated to me that he intended to resign not later than when the contract was let. He gave several reasons. He has been for the past three months, or for several weeks, at least, quite ill, and he has been pressing upon me more strongly than ever that he must resign. Finally, he, a few days ago, formally handed in his resignation. I regretted very much to accept his resignation. I had been endeavouring for months at different times to prevail upon him to remain on the board and take charge of the worrc until it was completed. I expect in a very short time to have the contract for the Quebec bridge superstructure signed. When that is done I will be pleased to bring down all the correspondence with reference to it as well as the correspondence concerning the resignation of the chief engineer.

Some time ago I noticed by press reports that the proposition now before the United States Congress to dam the St. Lawrence river had been defeated in the House of Representatives. I noticed subsequently that it had been reintroduced into the Senate and there are rumours to the effect that it is about to be forced through in the hurried work at the close of this session when everything is going through Congress very rapidly. Has the First Minister any information bearing on the matter and have any steps been taken by this government to induce the American Congress not to pass that legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have received no information at all upon the subject. We have taken certain action with respect to this matter which will be brought down to the House as soon as the correspondence-is completed.

I do not wish to have any state secrets from the First Min-

ister, but there has been a feeling throughout the Dominion that this is a very important matter. The Prime Minister has never yet intimated whether there has been a protest by the Canadian government on behalf of the Canadian people concerning this matter. The public undoubtedly believe that this is violating the Ashburton Treaty. I am surprised that the Prime Minister will not give the public information as to whether a formal protest has ever been made. It is all well enough to let the matter drift through Congress, but if the First Minister will inform the public that he has entered a formal protest to Washington that this Bill is violating the Ashburton Treaty, then if Congress pass it they are doing it in direct opposition to the protest made by the Prime Minister of Canada on behalf of Canada. In every reply made by the Prime Minister there has been hesitation as to expressing that fact. I cannot see for the life of me why there should be any hesitation. It is quite plain in the Ashburton treaty
The hon. genstleiman, cannot discuss the question on the orders of the day.

I simplv wish to ask whether the Prime Minister has definitely protested to the President of the . United States through Ambassador Bryce, against that Bill going through in violation of the Ashburton Treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have nothing to add to the information which I have given already. We have made representations to Mr. Bryce to convey to the American government. We have no intention of withdrawing what we have done, the report has been prepared and will be laid on the table of the House at a very early date, perhaps on Monday.

There is an understanding in some minds that article 7 of the Ashburton Treaty has been overridden by the legislation in connection with the Waterways Commission. Is the government in a position to give us any information in that regard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I want to draw the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that Congress will sit only for a few days longer, and one day next week is a holiday. The Prime Minister tells us that he will bring the papers down on Monday, perhaps. That does not mean that we are going to have them on Monday, and we have only a couple of days next week to consider the matter before Congress adjourns. There is no doubt that there never was a more important Bill brought before Congress in so far as the relations between Canada and the United States are concerned, and I cannot understand why the right hon. the Mr. REID (Grenville).
Prime Minister should not tell us what instructions he really gave the British ambassador, Mr. Bryce. No doubt these instructions are in the report, and it is only a question of bringing down the report and laying it on the table. If we had the information that the right hon. gentleman had instructed Mr. Bryce to notify the President that the passage of such a measure would be a violation of the Ashburton Treaty, that would be quite satisfactory, but we certainly should have information on that point. This is not the first time that the United States have not lived up to their treaty obligations towards Canada, and we therefore have reason to doubt that they might possibly fail to carry out the reciprocity arrangements now before this House, according to its spirit, if that arrangement should be adopted. If instances were wanting to prove my assertion that the United States government have not always kept faith with Canada, I could easily supply them.
Let me give one or two to show that the United States government have not kept faith with this country, although we have always kept faith with them. Some years ago a treaty was made providing for a reciprocal use of the canals by the two countries. Canada has lived up to that, treaty. For instance, a vessel can load at New York, go through the Erie canal and down through the Welland and thence to Ottawa, going through all our canals, and no one questions its right. But I have yet to learn that a Canadian vessel, laden in a Canadian port, has ever been allowed to go through to New York through the Erie canal. I challenge the right hon. the Prime Minister to point to one instance of a Canadian vessel laden in Canada being allowed to go through an American canal. I am informed by marine men that when a Canadian vessel gets to the dividing line, she must unload and transfer her cargo to an American bottom. The reason given by the American government for this breach of faith is that the American canals are owned by separate states. A Canadian vessel is not allowed to go' from St. John's to New York through the Erie canal because that canal belongs to the state of New7 York. Thus by simply, transferring their canals to the several states, the United States evade the provisions of a treaty made with Canada. Let me give another instance. According to treaty, no war vessels of either country are to be allowed on the Great Lakes. But what do we find? When the United States government applied for permission for war vessels to go through our canals, they told ug that if we did not give that permission they would abrogate the treaty; and rather than have the treaty abrogated, our gov-' ernment allowed these vessels the use of our canals, although of course without

guns. Let me cite still another instance. When the Canadian government said to the United States:	You are violating
treaty obligations by putting your war vessels on the lakes and thus giving you an advantage over us in case of war, the reply sent by Washington was this. They said: It is not we who are doing this, it is being done by the state of New York; these are training ships which we have given to the states of New York and Minnesota simply to be used for training purposes, and if you do not allow these vessels through your canals, each state will build its own training ships. Thus they fall back on state rights, which are equivalent to our provincial rights. In this way our American cousins evade their treaty obligations, and I could cite other instances. I might refer to the fisheries, but I am not going into any more detail. All I wish to point out is that while Canada has kept faith, the United States have not.
As respects the particular case which ] have brought to the attention of the House, it is as plain as possible that a similar evasion is sought to be practised. The Ashburton Treaty shows exactly what was agreed to between the two countries. In that connection a question has been raised about the dam built at Sheik island. Well, I have seen the maps and plans, and that_ part where Sheik island dam was built is not in the international arrangement at all. In fact the Ashburton Treaty was made after that dam was built, and, therefore, does not applv to it. The very fact that the President'of the United States would allow Congress to pass a Bill which is in direct violation of the treaty, would show bad faith on the part of the United States. We are now about to make an arrangement on this reciprocity question. I remember years ago when the United States put up barriers to prevent the carrying out of the arrangement then in force for letting our farm products go in free. By establishing United States consuls at the different points, to whom our people had to pay heavy consul fees, they managed to evade the agreement.
I cannot for one moment believe that when the Bill for the construction of this dam came before Congress, the right hon. the Prime Minister did not immediately wire Ambassador Bryce to notify the President of the United States that such a measure was a violation of the Ashburton Treaty. If the right hon. gentleman did that, he was doing his duty and his people would_ be satisfied. But if he did it, what objection has he to letting us know? He Hesitates, however, and will not give a direct answer, and that causes me to suspect that there is something concealed, something behind, which he does not wish to divulge. We know that some of the
strongest friends of the Prime Minister, some of his strongest supporters, are shoving this Bill through at Washington and here.
Any doubt about that?
Not the slightest, the Prime Minister knows it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not.

Well, he knows that the chief solicitor of this company is. Mr. Leighton McCarthy, who sat in parliament here at one time, who is one of: the right hon. gentleman's supporters, and helped to keep him in office.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As a lawyer, he does it.

He is doing it as a lawyer, and he has got thousands and thousands out of it already. He is here doing his best to shove this through the House, and as he is doing it as a lawyer, no one can blame him for doing it in that way. I am not finding fault with him for performing that duty, because that is a part of his profession as a lawyer. I do not wish to reflect upon him. At the same time, there is no doubt that he is putting pressure upon the minister and his supporters to try to get this Bill through. So, I would like the Prime Minister to give us this information without hesitation. There is no reason why he should hesitate. Should this matter turn out in the way I hope it will not turn out, and should it be found that the Prime Minister has hesitated to defend Canada's rights, even to the extent of asking the President of the United States to see to it that that treaty is carried out, we on this side, a.nd I believe many hon. members on the other side as well, will feel very sorry that that should be the position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have only to repeat what I said. The government have made representations to Mr. Bryce to be conveyed to the American authorities.
I have no hesitation in bringing down the papers. I said they would be brought down. In fact, I may inform the hon. gentleman that I hope to bring them down on Monday. The clerk of the Privy Council handed them to me, and I have them in my desk, but on looking through them I find that some lateT despatches are not among them. I hope to have these papers added, and to bring the whole down on Monday. And I hope that I shall not lose the goodly opinion of my hon. friend (Mr. Reid, Grenville) when he has had an opportunity to read the papers.
I have a word to say to the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He is one of the ministers who blushed-
What, what?

Yes, I reaffirm it- blushed-when the non. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) was stating {hat certain gentlemen on this side of the boundary and supporters of the Prime Minister were interested in pushing this thing through. Some strange things develop sometimes-
< So we see.

I do not know whether the evidence brought out before the committees at Washington might tend to throw light on this subject or not, but I think the First Minister might properly interest himself in studying some of the evidence which has been brought out before those committees on this very matter. It would prove very interesting reading to the public of Canada. There is a powerful organization behind this concern. Money has been spent, not in thousands or tens of thousands, but in hundreds of thousands-
Millions.
Make it billions.
I do not say that all this has come to this side of the line, but a good deal of it has.
Who got it?
Read the evidence as far as it has gone. It will all be produced.
Did you say ' Read ' the evidence?

The point I wish to impress on the First Minister is that there is no use locking the stable door after the horse is stolen. An ounce of prevention is woTth a nound of cure. Before that Bill passes the American Congress is the time for this parliament to take action. The government has been notified that legislation has been going on there, promoted by a private company, to interfere with waterways of Canada, in which we have a vital interest. The excuse is made, as I understand it, that the Ashburton Treaty gives them the right to do this. And the instance is cited of the little dam between Sheik island and the Canadian shore. But who * will pretend that this is on a par with a [DOT] dam 'between Long Sault island or Barn-Vnart island and the American shore? The 'iVshburton Treaty distinctly states that the channels on each side of Long Sault island and on each side of Barnhart island are *inviolable, but it never mentions, directly [DOT]or indirectly, the little channel between 'Sheik island and the Canadian shore. These important channels mentioned in the treaty are being interfered with by this proposition at Ottawa. The proposition is to dam the channel between Long Sault island and the American shore, to dam the channel between Barnhart island and Long Sault island, and then to dam the Mr. FOSTER.
channel between Barnhart island and the Canadian shore. (Yes, as a friend near me suggests, it is a doubly damned institution.) Under this proposition 95 per centres, 97 per cent, I am told-of the electric power will be on the American side. It is mere child's play for any minister of the Crown to tell us that if this legislation is passed at Washington and if these dams are made they will see to it that half the power is reserved for the Canadian side. If power is wanted there is any amount of power available where it will not interfere with navigation. Let them go down to the Coteau, the Cedars, or the Cascades. If they want power, and if you want to make a deal with them let them take the power where there is no navigation, but let them not interfere with the Long Sault channel. I saw by the press the other day that it was reported that, already the ice at Cornwall has raised the waters to the extent of 14 feet. If this proposed dam were built the ice floating down from the rapids above would accumulate, and there i's no saying what harm might be done. We know what these ice jams and bursts have caused in other parts of the world, - and there is no reason to doubt that the disaster caused at this point might be tremendous. But aside from that, there is the interference with the navigation of the river. This is an international channel, and should be preserved as it is. I am surprised that any minister of the Crown of the Dominion of Canada, any responsible person under the British flag, can be found dickering, or even for an instant considering, the question of closing that waterway. This is an important 'matter, and I would suggest to the Prime Minister-I suppose it would come within his department-to take the matter up. and not only protest against this action going further, but also get copies of the evidence before the committee in Washington and look into the matter. My faith in him is such that 1 believe that if he had that evidence before him now he would put his foot down and settle the question. Now is the time to stop it. In the United States such Bills as this are slipped through sometimes, just as they are here, without much attention being paid to them. However, so far as we are concerned, vie are on our guard. We have had the warning of a certain Bill which was passed through this House. But we are on our guard, and I think that, for the next few years at all events, until suspicion is lulled, there will be pretty close watch kept on the legislation affecting matters along the border. Knowing the danger, it is certainly the duty of this government to protest and to protest in most emphatic language, against the reiritroduction of this Bill before the Congress at Washington.

I presume that when the correspondence is brought down my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) will see that even his visit to Washington was not necessary to protect the rights of Canada. He let slip one word very significant to me, that there were other water-powers available in that vicinity. I know there are, and we in eastern Ontario hope to get power from some source even if the Sault is never developed. So far as his reference to me is concerned, I am not alarmed about that. But I rose mainly to say a word in answer to my hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid). I think that he is in error as to the United States not giving us reciprocal treatment in the use of their canals. The hon. member for ATgenteuil (Mr. Perley), I think it was, brought this matter up, discussing correspondence he had had with the State Department, if I remember correctly. At his suggestion, I wrote to the head of the canal department of the state of New York. Speaking from memory, that authority assured me that the canals were free and open to the vessels of Canada, if they desired to use them, as much as to their own vessels, and that the authorities never charged any canal dues on Canadian vessels. I want to make that statement, because I believe it is fair to the United States and to the state of New York.

Do I understand now, that a Canadian vessel can load at a Canadian port and go directly to New York with a cargo of freight P I suppose these little fishing yachts are allowed to go through, I do not refeT to them. Am I right in understanding now that there is no doubt that a vessel can load at Ottawa, for instance, go through the Welland canal, on down through the Erie canal to New York, without breaking cargo, so long as the cargo is consigned from Ottawa direct to New York ? I ask that question, because one of the largest marine men told me that their vessels were compelled to unload. If that is not the case, then I will inform1 this marine man, who told me, that he is entirely in error, and I will give the reply of the Minister of Railways 'and Canals.

The information, as 1 remember it, which I received last year from the head of the canal department of the state of New York, is that Canadian vessels have the same free access to their canals as their own vessels.
They have under federal law, but not under state law.

I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), to a matter of very serious importance to the navigation of Lake Winnipeg. Last year, owing to an early frost,
all the vessels, except one, were frozen in on Lake Winnipeg. This was a very serious matter, and has entailed great loss to owners of steamboats, and endangered the lives of a great many men employed on these boats. The remedy would be-for the government to have a boat sufficiently strong at Selkirk, or at the mouth of the river, to keep the river open. I have a resolution here from the Board of Trade at Selkirk, which I wish to place on record. I understand it has already been placed in the hands of the Minister of Public Works:
IN hereas all vessels of draught operating upon the waters of Lake Winnipeg require to and do frequently enter the mouth and travel upon the waters of the Red river in order to reach the town of Selkirk, which is the chief harbour and port of entry for Lake Winnipeg, and where all the vessels of the lake have their winter berth and repair station; and
Whereas, owing to the geographical configuration of this portion of the American continent, the Red river of the north will always continue to be the navigable highway and avenue of approach to and exit from Lake Winnipeg for vessels of draught; and
Whereas the navigation of Lake Winnipeg, and the shipping industry of the lake are vast enterprises, having invested therein great sums of money and giving employment to many hundreds of people; and that this industry, and its relative importance to Canada is undoubtedly to greatly increase in the future; and
Whereas the government of the Dominion of Canada has in its wisdom recognized the importance of the navigation of trade and commerce on this lake and its connecting river, and through its Department of Public Works has appropriated and expended great sums of money, and has employed pronounced engineering skill upon the task of maintaining, improving and extending and rendering less hazardous the navigation of this body of water, and does now maintain at Selkirk an important depot of the Department of Public Works for such purpose; and
Whereas all vessels engaged in the fishing industry or in providing for the wants and necessities of those engaged in that industry are compelled, by the very nature of their calling, to ply the lake as late as possible in the fall; this necessity applying especially to the men and vessel or vessels engaged in the collection of spawn for the charging of the fish hatcheries maintained by the government for the perpetuity of the species; and
Whereas the Red river freezes and bocomes closed to navigation some time before the waters of the lake freezes and becomes closed, and that by this circumstance the vessels plying upon the lake are, some years, and especially this year, prevented by ice from entering the Red river, and are compelled to make shift as best they can for the winter upon the open lake, thereby causing great delay, inconvenience and hazard and direct loss; and
Whereas the situation at present upon the lake is that vessels of steam draught, including the government tug, 'Lady of the Lake.' and including all the steam vessels engaged
The question of building wharfs on Lake Winnipeg has been referred to the Committee of Supply. I should think that my hon. friend would be out of order in discussing this matter now.
Well, I was just referring to this in connection with the other matter. Of course, if I am out of order-
My hon. friend will have ample opportunity when we come to those items.
I would like to urge the minister
I presume he will have an opportunity again in Supply.

I presume I will if I am in the House, but I would like to urge upon the minister the necessity of making provision for these urgent improvements, and if he is not in a position to make a definite statement to the House to-day 1 trust he will do so when the time comes to discuss the estimates. I thought 1 had his pledge last year, but it was not carried out.

Some time ago the petition of which my hon. friend has read a copy, was sent to me from the Board of Trade of Selkirk, and I also received a request from the secretary of the Board of Trade of Winnipeg urging that an icebreaker should be provided for the purpose of breaking the ice at the mouth of the Red river and also at Lake Winnipeg. As the matter of employing tugs for ice-breaking purposes in other sections of Canada had been attended to by the Department of Marine and Fisheries and not by the Department of Public Works I referred the petition to my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and advised the Selkirk Board of Trade and also the secretary of the Board of Trade of Winnipeg that the matter was one which did not appertain, in my opinion, to my department but appertained to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The tug ' Whelan/ which is employed for breaking the ice in the harbour of Port Arthur and Fort William and perhaps at other points on Lake Superior, is employed by the Department of Marine and Fisheries and not by the Department of Public Works, and so it is with regard to ice-breaking upon the St Lawrence. The matter rests entirely with the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I have referred the matter to my colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; he is not in his place at the present moment, but I have no doubt the question will receive his very careful consideration. I shall take occasion to call his attention to the remarks which my hon. friend has made and which will appear in ' Hansard ' where he will have an opportunity of seeing them. I think that on his behalf I can say to my hon. friend that the matter will receive very careful consideration. We all recognize the great importance of the Red river between the city of Winnipeg and its mouth and also the great importance of Lake Winnipeg and also the importance of doing what we reasonably can to assist The navigation of the lake and the Red river and of making navigation as safe as possible. Therefore. I am sure my hon. friend can rely upon the request of" the Selkirk people receiving very careful consideration.

I notice the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) in his place now. I was just drawing the attention of the House to the Matter of providing a boat for keeping the Red river

open. I understand that the chief engineer of the Department of Marine and Fisheries was sent up to investigate and the word that I got from Selkirk was that he stated that it was a matter for the Public Works Department. That is why I referred my remarks to the Minister of Public Works to-day. There is a very urgent request and resolution and I would like to know if the minister can give me any encouragement that that boat will be provided for that important work.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No report has yet been made to me with regard to this ice breaker When the question was brought to my attention some time ago I gave immediate instructions to have a report made. That report has not yet reached me. As soon as I get it I shall communicate it to my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to a letter which I received yesterday, and which reads:	,
Cambro, Ont., Feb. 21. 1911. Mr. F. R. Lalor, M.P.,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Lalor,-When I wrote you yesterday I had not read the report of the debate-

I do not think the
hon. gentleman can refer to that now because we are going into Supply, while the subject to which the letter refers has been referred to the Committee on Ways and Means. I think it would be irregular now to read the letter.
It is a correction about a statement made in the House.
As a correction of a statement I presume it would be admissible.

The letter reads:
When I wrote you yesterday I had not read the report of the debate in the House regarding reciprocity, and I notice on page 3826 that the hon. Mr. Paterson replying to Mr. Arm-stiong states 'that the Dairy Association of Eastern and Western Ontario unanimously desired that this treaty should go into affect.'
This statement is absolutely incorrect in so far as the Dairymens' Association of Western Ontario is concerned. I am a director of that association land hake been for over twenty years. I was present in Stratford when this question w-as introduced. The facts are as follows:	After the convention was
opened a couple of farmers came to myself and one or two others, asking that we put this question on our programme to be discussed during the convention, before deciding in regard to the advisability of doing so. We consulted every director and officer of the association and we unanimously agreed not to permit the question to go on the programme of the convention for discussion. As there Mr. BRADBURY.
was not one man on the board who believed the measure would be in the best interest of the dairy industry of this province, we told these men that if they wished to discuss this question they would have to do so altogether independent of the association. They then asked permission to bring this question up at the close of the afternoon session of the first day of the convention, this was granted and after the session of the convention was closed, a gentleman on the floor of the convention hall moved and another seconded his resolution, that Mr. Scott our president act *as chairman while those present would discuss the question of reciprocity. Mr. Scott was accordingly elected chairman of the meeting, when these two iren, Mr. Behn of Oxford county and Mr. Rice of Norfolk county, introduced a resolution that they believed it would be in the best interests of the dairy industry of this country, to have reciprocity between the United States and Canada. In the discussion of this question there was not one word spoken by any officer of the Dairymens' Association of Western Ontario in favour of it, and there was not one who voted for the resolution, in fact there was less than twenty in the entire audience who voted for the resolution.
I thought I would give you these facts, so that if the opportunity presented itself you cc-uld put the Minister of Customs right in regard to the attitude of the Dairymens' Association of Western Ontario.
Sincerely yours,
J.	N. PAGET.

On the 7th of December last, I asked a question with regard to the proposed highway bridge between Hawkes-bury, Ontario, and Grenville, Quebec. In repiy the minister said:
With reference to the bridge across the Ottawa river at Hawkesbury, Ont., the delay in this matter has been on account of the approach to the bridge on the Ontario side.
He went, on to say that this was the natural place for the crossing to be made and afterwards said:
Although I do not think there is anything in writing, it has been understood all along, or at least expected, that the town of Hawkesbury would arrange with the Hawkesbury Lumber Company for a right of way through their property giving an approcah to the bridge and, I may say, it is the custom for municipalities to do this.
The minister explained there was some trouble between the town of Hawkesbury and the Hawkesbury Lumber Company in regard to their assessment, and that was probably the reason why nothing had been done. There is a special and peculiar need for a bridge across the Ottawa at this particular point. There is no highway bridge across Die Ottawa river below the city of Ottawa and the consequence is that the people up and down the Ottawa river on both sides would use this bridge if it were built. In the summer they get along very well

with ferries, and in the middle of winter by using the ice, but between seasons, in the fall and spring, there is always a longer or shorter period when it is impossible for any one to cross the Ottawa with safety. The consequence is that there have been a great many accidents in the fall and spring and people have lost their lives in attempting to cross the river. This matter was all laid before the minister I think twice and all these reasons given, and the minister stated he believed it was in the public iinterest that this bridge should be built. I submit that the reason given by the minister in this answer for not going on. with the building of the bridge is a poor one. He states that it is the custom for the municipalities to arrange for the right of way for such bridges.
No, for the highway to the bridge, the approach to the bridge.
For the right of way to the bridge.
That is to connect with the main highway.	*

For the right of way to the bridge. I doubt very much whether there is any such custom, and I do not think the minister can show that there is in cases of this kind. If it is in the public interest that the bridge should be built the authorities who are to build the bridge must surely provide the approaches to the bridge as well as the bridge itself. I am surprised at the minister giving a reason of that kind, when I remember what he has stated in this House several times with reference to the public buildings which he is putting up in this country. Not long ago when a public building was being discussed the minister stated with great emphasis that he would never think of asking a municipality to provide a site for the building, and surely there is more reason why the government should provide the approaches to a bridge which is evidently in the public interest.
Why not build one like the Disraeli bridge?
I leave that to the min-:ister.
It is hardly courageous to do that. Why does not the hon. gentleman reply to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule)?
The minister is well able to take care of himself, and the kind of bridge provided at Disraeli did not throw any credit on the minister's department.
The hon. member for East Grey is trying to throw ridicule on this bridge and the member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) should resent that.

Not at all, the hon. member for East Grey is bringing to the attention of the minister the fact that he built a bridge for a municipality and called it a wharf, he showed himself willing to do ' that in Disraeli even although it did not come within his proper scope.
The minister did not happen to do that.

If the land belonging to the Hawkesbury Lumber Company should be expropriated for this bridge, it seems to me the minister should go on and take the necessary proceedings to expropriate. If, on the contrary, it is considered best that the bridge should be put somewhere else under the circumstances, to serve the people of these two counties, I have a map of that section of the river and there are other places where a bridge could be built. I think something should be done about that. The bridge is a great necessity, it is not a matter of politics at all, it has been taken up by all sections of the people, and has been agreed to by the minister. I want to urge on the minister to take steps to get this bridge built as soon as possible and I will ask him if he will not do so.

It is quite true that this bridge has been decided upon. It is to be built at the joint expense of the governments of Quebec, Ontario and the Dominion, the Dominion contributing the lion's share. When this matter was urged upon me, as it was very strongly, by the hon. gentleman who represents the constituency on the Quebec side with the hon. member for the county of Prescott, I w>as led to understand that the municipality would be likely to provide the highway, giving the approach to the bridge. I rather inferred also that the Hawkesbury Lumber company were likely to give a right of way through their property, either free or at a low cost, Since that time, some difficulty has arisen between the Hawkesbury Lumber company and the town of Hawkesbury. I believe the assessment of the company's property has been considerably raised, and they have not towards the town council, the same good feeling which they had when this bridge was originally proposed. My own view is, that it is not at all unreasonable, when the three governments are undertaking, at a large expense, to build a bridge for the accommodation of the people of the locality that the municipality should provide a highway that would give the approach to the bridge from the main highway. That has been done in other cases. However, I am not without hope that the previously friendly relations between the company and the town may be restored, and that the arrangement, as originally proposed, may be carried out. If in the coming spring that appears unlikely to take place, then it will be my duty to consider the question of obtaining another

location for the bridge. I hesitate about expropriating a right of way through the company's property without its consent. This might involve the Crown in an expense away beyond what we bad anticipated the bridge would cost us. I intend to take the matter up in the spring or early summer, in the hope that a satisfactory arrangement may be arrived at.

I may say that I was at two meetings, and I never noticed that there was any arrangement, express or implied, by which the Hawkesbury Lumber company would give , a free right of way or a right of way at a low cost. Is the minister quite sure that there was such an understanding ?
Perhaps the hon. member for Prescott, who is familiar with the details of the matter, can give some information with regard to it.

I understand that the Hawkesbury Lumber company have never promised a right of way, but we bad hoped that the town council would arrange with the company to get a right of way. Last year the town had a lawsuit with the company about the assessment, and the company were not disposed to grant the right of way. They told the Hawkesbury Bridge Committee that if they wanted the right of way, they would have to expropriate. I think it is still their intention that the government or the town will have to expropriate the right of way.
Then the Hawkesbury Lumber company's refusal .to grant the right of way had nothing to do with the dispute between them and the town regarding taxes ?
No. The assessment of the company was increased before there was a request made to it by the town.

I notice in the Ottawa ' Free Press,' of this date, the following reference to myself:
In the House of Commons yesterday, Dr. Clark secured from Mr. Bradbury, the Conservative member for Selkirk, an admission that he was opposed to reciprocity and a declaration that the men who hail organized the grain growers' deputation in December last were members of a ' political machine.'
I want to say that this is a misconstruction of what I said. What I did say was, that the Grain Growers' organization'was the. political end of the grain growers' of Manitoba. The article goes on to say:
Now, human memory is often erratic, but it comes to our mind that when the great grain growers' delegation was nearing Ottawa to demand reciprocity, a deputation of western Conservative M.P.'s went 'up the line' to meet Mr. PUGSLEY.
them, and to extend the hand of co-operation against ' the tariff tyranny of the Liberal government's tariff. There were eight of them and they may have included George Bradbury. They certainly included the other leaders of Conservative opinion west of the lakes, and as there are only a dozen of them all told, it is a fair presumption that George Bradbury was one of the contingent. He was certainly active enough when the delegates were down here in endeavouring to impress upon them the opinion that he was heart and soul in sympathy with their demands.
Now, I just want to say that when the delegation were here, their demand was not for reciprocity, but for a reduction of duties, and I was in hearty sympathy with that demand.
What has happened since to change his views? Has the word come from the twin bosses of Manitoba, Rogers and Roblin, that the grain growers are to he thrown to the wolves and are to be represented as a body of disloyal annexationists?
I want to say just a word regarding my attitude when the delegation was here. I was in hearty sympathy with the demand of the Grain Growers' Association when they were asking this government for a reduction of the duty on farm implements, which is something that every man from Manitoba on this side of the House supports. The question of reciprocity is another question. I did not say that I was opposed to reciprocity. I stated that I was opposed to reciprocity, as proposed by the present government. I am absolutely opposed to it, and I want my constituents to know it. I want my constituents to know it, for I am not going behind doors. My opposition is open and above board.
What kind of reciprocity?

I will tell you when the time comes. What I want to do is to set the ' Free Press ' right, which I am sure has no intention of misrepresenting me or putting a false construction on my attitude. There is no man from the west, Manitoba or the territories, who has stood out more firmly for the rights of the farmers than I have. When a resolution was before the Chair asking for what the farmers require more than reciprocity, namely, government-owned and operated terminal elevators, the Conservative members were found standing by my hon friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) and endeavouring to induce the government to adopt the resolution moved by him. They have also been found standing by the farmers in other matters, which are more important to the agriculturists of Manitoba and the west than this question of reciprocity as proposed by this government. I have no hesitation in saying that this proposition

of the government is simply a gold brick offered the farmers of the northwest, and it will not be my fault if they do not find it out before it is too late.

I would ask the Minister of Labour if he has had any communication asking for certain amendments to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act of 1907?
I received yesterday from one of the hon. members of this House a communication transmitting some proposed amendment. That is the only one I have received this session to that effect.

I have received a communication from the Moyie Miners' Union No. 71 with regard to clause 56 of the Act. They suggest that this clause should be amended to read as follows:
Provided, that it shall be unlawful for any employer, incorporated company or corporation to close down their industries and than resume operations under changed conditions of employment, without first giving prominent notice in the local newspaper at least thirty days prior to the resumption of operations.
The object of this is to prevent an evasion of the Act. Under clause 56 it is unlawful to have a lockout, but the same thing has been brought about in another way. An employer may, for instance, close down his works, without giving any particular reason or possibly for some reason entirely outside the matter in dispute, and then, when it suits him, reopen it under changed conditions. Has the attention of the minister been called to that particular weakness in the Act?

The same proposition came in the communication I received from the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell). I shall certainly consider it very carefully. My impression at the moment is that if action of that kind were taken the company would be liable, undeT the Act as it stands. If my contention be right there is no need to amend the Act, but that is a matter on which I should like to have the opinion of the Justice Department.

I agree that the object of the Act is to prevent any such violation, but evidently the labour organizations have not found it altogether effective. Possibly the minister, after considering the wording
of the Act. may deem it necessary to amend it in the way suggested. I am very glad that he is taking the question up with the Justice Department, and trust that if he finds what is pointed out is really the case he will make the necessary amendment. [DOT]

How many copies of the ' Labour Gazette ' are printed, and to whom are they sent? How many correspondents are there, and how are they paid? Where is the ' Labour Gazette ' printed and bound and what does the printing and binding cost?

In the .vicinity of 16,000 copies are published every month. There is a paid subscription list of pearly 10,000. A distribution is made to members of both Houses, copies are sent out occasionally for the purpose of getting other subscriptions, free copies are also sent to departments of government in other countries ai'd to newspapers m exchange for their publications; also to the public libraries educational institutions, labour organizations and Boards of Trade.
Are they sent to every newspaper in the country?

Yes. The number of correspondents is 52, and they are paid $100 each per year. They are occasionally called upon to make special reports. For example, the department may be collecting information as to prices and the cost of living. This is in the nature of additional work to their regular duties, and, in such cases, an extra allowance is made to these correspondents of $25 for the work done in that connection through the year. I do not recollect if there were any other questions-
What revenue does the government receive from those who subscribe to the ' Labour Gazette? '
Last year, the revenue from this source was $1,547.
Is the subscription price $1 a year?
No, 20 cents a year.
I understood there were 16,000 copies issued. The figures would indicate tiiat about 10,009 copies were paid for, leaving 6,0uu tree.
Yes.
I hardly think the explanation the minister has given would account for these 6,000 copies.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. iSchaffner) understands that there are copies kept in the department for purposes of binding and to meet future demands. There are also some 1,800 labour organizations in the country, and many newspapers. There is also a large exchange.

list. I might say the ' Labour Gazette ' is sent to the different statistical bureaus of European countries, and other countries throughout the world.
I suppose the minister could state the numbers used in these ways?

I have the figures here. Last year the exchange list of departments of government, including federal, provincial and British and foreign governments num-. bered 509; trade papers and labour journals 167 ; public libraries and libraries of educational institutions 125 ; members of the House of Commons, 221 ; members of the Senate, 87 ; boards of trade, 276 ; newspapers, 1,075 ; labour organizations-Nova Scotia, 160 ; Prince Edward Island, 11 ; New Brunswick, 83, Quebec (copies sent both in English and in French) 610 ; Ontario, 770 ; Manitoba, 106 ; Saskatchewan.. 14 ; Alberta, 131 ; British Columbia, 222; a total of labour organizations, 2,174. This is a larger number than I thought.
I would like the minister to give the House some information as to the object of this * Labour Gazette.' What is its purpose?

Before the minister goes on with that, I would like him to finish answering the questions I asked. I asked where the ' Labour Gazette ' was printed, and whether the work was done by tender or not, how many copies were printed, and the cost of printing?

That question, I am afraid I would have to refer to the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy). The department of labour makes its contract with the government Printing Bureau for the printing of the; ' Labour Gazette.' Accounts are sent by the Printing Bureau to the Labour Department, and paid by the department. I understand that the ' Labour Gazette ' is printed at the ' Free Press ' printing office in this city, but that is by arrangement which the King's Printer has made in accordane with rules made at the Bureau.
