I have here the figures oi the cost of printing the ' Labour Gazette ' for the last fiscal year. The ' Labour Gazette ' is printed in both English and French. The printing of the English edition cost $11,544.80, of the French edition $5,704.16. In addition to printing the ' Gazette,' at the end of each year the ' Gazette ' is bound, and an index is prepared for the use of subscribers, and this costs $190.07. That cost includes the paper.

So the cost per volume of these twelve copies for the year is $1.20 for printing, and as the minister gives it to subscribers for 20 cents a year, subscribers get off pretty cheap under those circumstances. Perhaps it is the intention that the ' Labour Gazette ' should not be self-supporting?

I may say that in some countries similar publications are distributed free of charge. The purpose in fixing any amount is not to bring in a revenue at all; it is simply to insure the fact that whoever gsks for the ' Gazette ' is likely to have some Teal desire for it.
Who makes terms with the ' Free Press,' or whatever concern prints it?

I understand the King's Printer fixes the terms in accordance with

a rule lie adopts at the Government Printing Bureau. There is a rule governing all printing which is done outside, and the King's Printer follows this rule with regard to the ' Labour Gazette.'

I must congratulate the Minister of Labour on his extreme liberality. I wish some other departments would take this leaf out of his book. I had occasion a few days ago to ask the Minister of Agriculture for a copy of the bulletin with respect to seeds in Canada, and 1 received from him a very courteous reply -I do not complain of it at all-telling me that I had had three copies before, and if I would send a dollar down to the King's Printer I could get another copy. I asked it for a friend, perhaps that was the reason wdiy he suggested that I should pay a dollar for it. If I had not mentioned that probably he might have given it. But I wanted it for a student at the Guelph Agricultural College, who desired to make use of it in preparing for his examination. I put it that way to the Minister of Agriculture, thinking, perhaps, I would appeal to his generosity. But he appears to have no respect for students at agricultural colleges, at any rate he does not treat them in the same way that the Minister of Labour treats his friends. I merely make mention of this in the House to give it all the publicity I can, because I think it was a very small matter on the part of the Minister of Agriculture.
Would the Minister of Labour please tell us some of the purposes that this ' Labour Gazette ' is intended to subserve?

The main purpose is to gather information in regard to the industrial and labour conditions of the Dominion, and in respect to all matters likely to be of concern to employers and employees. This information is gathered by means of correspondents, who send in monthly reports. These 'correspondents are located in different cities of the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The trade journals and the press are carefully reviewed, and any items that appear to have a bearing upon labour conditions are carefully classified and compiled in the department. Statistics are also collected by special investigation, these are made up in the form of tabular statements. For example, each month the ' Labour Gazette ' contains a review of the industrial and labour conditions of the particular industries, agriculture, mining, lumbering and the like. Then it takes up the conditions in different trades, and this information is prepared in accordance with general form, beginning at the Atlantic and running across the continent. Then there is information of a special
nature; for example, industrial accidents, statistics gathered and classified, and at the end of the year a statement is made up showing the total number of these accidents and the causes in each case. A similar method is followed in regard to strikes and lockouts. Also, changes in rates of wages and changes in hours of labour, formation of employers labour organizations, so far as is possible to get them, are mentioned and classified and compiled, also, legal decisions affecting labour, &c. All data of this kind is so shaped at the outset that at the end of the year it may be possible to make statistical tables that will show the trend of industrial development for that year. Then, over a period of years the intention is to classify still further, in some cases in the form of charts, and these charts are printed in the annual report, or in special publications. I have m my hand the bound volume of the * Labour Gazette ' from July, 1909, to 1910. It is a volume of 1,500 pages with a carefully prepared index. To show the- scope of the work, I might read some of the subjects in the index :	Industrial accidents, adulteration of foods, arbitration, annuities, meetings of labour associations, building trades, accidents, changes in wages, hours of labour, &c. That is the nature of the information. The department has in mind, in gathering and compiling this information, to furnish the country with what would serve as a basis of an industrial history of the Dominion. There is no attempt to express opinions in the ' Gazette '; it is simply a compilation of data, which can be used by persons who desire it for reference.

I understand that the reports are sent in by agents all over the country, and these are edited in the department, and the department sends out what they see fit, and suppresses what they see fit. I think any one who reads the ' Labour Gazette ' must come to the conclusion that one of the chief objects of its existence is to advertise the department.

There is no intention to advertise the department. There is a desire to have the department's work known to the country. It would be of very little service to the community if the community knew nothing about it. To that extent, I suppose, the department follows the practice of any other organization.
I would like to ask the minister what principle is followed in the selection of the places to be served by correspondents ?

The department has tried to follow a general rule and confine the appointment of correspondents to localities that are either incorporated cities, or that have a population of 10,000 or more, and in some cases, where it has appeared that there are large industrial interests that could not be covered in that way, a district has been mapped out and a correspondent has been appointed for that particular district.
Would the minister say whether he has a correspondent at Prince Rupert, and if not, whether he thinks a correspondent there would give useful service.

The department has no correspondent at the present time at Prince Rupert, but I think the suggestion that my hon. friend makes, if he intends it as a suggestion, is one worthy of careful consideration. Prince Rupert promises to be an important centre, and I think I might say to my hon. friend that if he cares to Tecommend the appointment of a correspondent there, I would be prepared to appoint one.
As Prince Rupert is in the district represented by the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman), it might come with rather bad grace on my part to make any recommendation

I would be prepared to accept it.
Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster)

but certainly it is a point where, I think, there should be a correspondent of the ' Labour Gazette,' because there are a great many problems connected with labour constantly demanding attention and, although an officer of the labour department went to Prince Rupert during last year and made a very interesting report on conditions there, I think it would be well to supplement that report with regular monthly reports from a correspondent, because at Prince Rupert conditions are in a formative state, and they are not so well regulated as they are in older communities. It seems to me that this is one point Mr. SCHAFFNER.
where the services of a correspondent ought to be more valuable than at general points.
I notice that the ' Labour Gazette ' bears the union label.
Yes.
Is it printed in a union shop ?
I cannot say offhand whether the shop that prints it is a union shop or not, as I have not inquired into the question.
What authority would you have to put the union label on, if it were not printed in a union shop P
I understand that the conditions that prevail at the bureau are conditions that the union regard as satisfactory, or as coming up the standard.

The Minister of Labour certainly understands what I mean by asking if this is a union shop. I want to know if every man who works in this shop, is a union man and whether this label is rightly put on the ' Gazette ' or whether it is put on in some irregular way, to indicate that it comes from a union shop when, as a matter of fact, it may not.

As I understand, the union label is controlled by the Allied Printing Trades, and they allow its use by shops that comply with the conditions. I presume the shop that prints the ' Labour Gazette ' must comply with those conditions, or those who control the label would not have permitted it to be used by that shop.
Then they would have the consent of the Allied Printing Trades ?
Yes.

This item also refers to the conciliation of labour, and I would like to ask a few questions with reference to that. I think it has already been stated in connection with some of the strikes in Nova Scotia that the only difficulty about their settlement is, that the companys have decided that they will not hire men who happen to be members of a certain organization and that -they will not employ them unless they belong to some other organization that they may designate. To make my meaning plain, I understand that the United Mine Workers' Association is the association which prevails in Springhill, Nova Scotia, and that a large number of men in the county of Cape Breton also belong to that organization. I understand that the management of the Springhill company have decided that they will not employ men who are members of the United Mine Workers' Association.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Crosby) is mistaken in that view of it. At least I have been informed by Mr. Butler, who is the present manager of the Springhill mines, that he has no objection to the men belonging to whatever organization they please. They may belong to the United Mine Workers' Association if they wish to do so, but he is not prepared to deal with them as union men. He allows them the privilege of belonging to the union if they wish to do so, but he refuses to enter into an agreement with, the union as a union. That is the posi-1 tion as Mr. Butler stated it to me only a few weeks ago.

That being the case, has Mr. Butler, or Mr. Anybody Else, any right to dictate to the workingmen as to what organization they may belong to so long as the organization does not conflict with the interests of, or become a nuisance to, the employers of labour? Would they be acceptable to him if they belonged to the Provincial Workingmen's Association?

As I understand it, Mr. Butler does not raise the .question, in taking a man into his employ, whether he belongs to the Provincial Workingmen's Association or the United Mine Workers' Association. He stated that it was a matter of indifference to him whether the men were members of a Provincial Workingman's Association or of the United Mine Workers' Association; the contract he would make with them would be a contract irrespective of the organization to which they belonged. He would allow every workingman to join whatever organization he pleased, but he did not propose to confine his own liberty in the matter of taking men into employment to taking men belonging to any particular organization, and refusing to take men who might belong to another organization.

It is evident from the information I have received from the minister that the whole thing hinges on this small, miserable Question of whether a man belongs to this organization or to another organization, and that Mr. Butler, at the head of the Springhill mines will not treat with some men because they belong to a workingman's association headed by some letters instead of an organization headed by some other letters. I appeal to the Minister of Labour to exercise some influence with these men. It must be remembered that the coal mined by the Springhill company is owned by the people of the province of Neva Scotia, and is worked by that company under lease for a certain time under certain conditions. It is true that these conditions are made by our local legislature, but it must be remembered that 134
we have in the Dominion government a Department of Labour whose duty it is to deal with matters affecting the interests of labour. I was very pleased when that department was established and a spec'ai minister with full cabinet rank, placed at its head. The more you can do to improve the conditions of labour and of labouring men, the better it is for the country in which those men reside. It seems to me very petty for a company receiving a charter and a lease under which it mines this coal, to declare what is practically a lockout on the question of what labour union or organization the men shall belong to. Since the amalgamation of the Dominion Coal Company with the Springhill Company it is necessary for the men to combine together in such a way that they may be able to off set that great combination of capital. It has been said by Mr. Butler, the new manager, for whom I have a great respect, that he considers this question of whether the men do or do not belong to the United Mine Workers, a childish one. If it is childish why should this great financial combination say so and say to the men:	Go to work. Then we will have
the men at work instead of being locked out with a constant continuation of strife existing in one of the most prosperous districts of Nova Scotia. The late manager, Mr. Cowan, stated when the strike was brought on that the company was quite pleased to have it as they were not making money and were glad to have the mines closed, but that apparently was not altogether correct because the company concluded they must get the mine going and they commenced to get labour and carry on the work. I appeal to the minister to get this thing settled. I have personal knowledge that the only question in the way is this one of the men belonging to the United Mine Workers' Association, and it is a mere quibble to say that that is sufficient to justify the continuation of the strike. We have really had more trouble since the inauguration of the Labour Department than before. I am sorry to have to say that, but it is true and I do hope that the minister of Labour will make very strenuous efforts to bring about a settlement. There have been a number of boards of conciliation on this strike, but apparently it has not been possible to act on or enforce the report of any one of these boards. If that is the case, then the boards were simply a means of spending money. The men would have as much right to object to the amalgamation of the two coal companies as the coal companies have to say to what labour organization the men should belong.
Would it not be perfectly proper for the employee to say that because these two companies have amalgamated he would not work for either of them.

The workingmen are not saying that. My statement is that the coal being mined by these companies belongs to the province of Nova Scotia, that under the terms of their lease they are to carry on mining under certain conditions; therefore it is more or less like a public franchise, and 1 say that the miner or workingman would have as much right to say that there should be no combination cl companies, as the companies have a right to say to these men, because you have formed yourselves into an organization for the protection of yourselves, your homes and your families, we will not treat with you as an organization, and you must disband and separate yourselves from it before we will treat with you at all. To my mind that is a miserable quibble which ho self-respecting company should use; but if the companies say that, it is up to the government of the province of Nova Scotia and the government of the Dominion of Canada to see to it that the people who are assisting these companies to make the money which pays the dividends on many millions of watered stock, shall get their rights; and the only way they can get their rights as workingmen is to be returned to their work in the mines. It is only a quibble to object to their organization being headed by the letters United Mine Workers or Provincial Workingmen's Association or any other letters, so long as the organization is open to the public. I have every hope that before many days are over the Minister of Labour will be able to tell us that the men have returned to wprk, or give us some reason why they have not, because after all the boards that have sat on this question there should be some decision by this time. If the Minister of Labour finds that it is essential for him to communicate with the government of the province of Nova Scotia on this matter, I hope that within a very short! time the influence of the two governments will result in our people being put back to work. If it does, it will be an advantage not only to the province of Nova Scotia, but to the Dominion of Canada at large.

We might put through the other clauses, and then let the Bill stand. That would save time.
Then, the minister (Mr. Graham), I suppose, will take up this expropriation question with the promoter of the Bill and try to gex that clause in better shape.

Better let that clause stand and go on with the others.
On section 11,

When the committee rose we had under consideration the matter of the action or inaction of the Board of Conciliation in connection with the Springhill strike. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby) was laying down a principle as to which, I think we ought to hear from the Minister of Labour.
The subject of the Spring-hill strike was brought up me other day. when we were in committee, and has already been discussed three times.

At Springhill, as I understand it, the matter at issue was the recognition of a union and the question raised by the hon. member for Halifax was whether or not this department had made any endeavour to secure recognition of the union by the proprietors of the mine where the trouble occurred or 1341
whether the department took the opposite
view and stood behind the mine owxiers in declining to treat with the men ; on that basis 1 think we ought to hear from the minister with regard to that point.

I have no hesitation in stating that the recognition or non-recognition of a union is something to be entirely left to the parties themselves. The department would not be justified in asking the employers to recognize the union any mora than in asking the employees to take any particular stand against the employers who failed to recognize the union. That is a matter to be left to the parties themselves. I said once before that I did not know anything short of -a law which would make it illegal for men to strike because of the non-recognition of a union, or for employers to lock out because of men joining a union that could meet such a situation. I do not think the House would enact such a law.

I did not suggest the enactment of the law. What I asked was merely the principle upon which the department proceeds, because if the department is really wedded to the idea that employers should not recognize unions, then its services would be of no value at all to the men in disputes such as have been referred to. If, on the other hand, the department were of the opinion that a recognition of the unions is in the interest of the workingmen, and would give friendly advice in a general way to the corporations brought before the Board of Conciliation, it might be of great service indeed to the mass of the people, and I take it that this department has been organized for the special protection of the mass of the people against more powerful influences that do not need the services of any department to protect them. I would ask the minister whether he accepts it as part of his duty to endeavour to influence corporations generally to recognize the unions, or whether he stands for the nonrecognition of unions on the part of corporations.

Every case depends on the circumstances surrounding it. In some cases it might be advisable to try to persuade a corporation to recognize the union as a means of helping to settle industrial disputes ; in other cases it might not be expedient. It is not a matter upon which one can generalize.
Then it is safe to say that as a general rule the minister does not lend his influence to secure the recognition of unions by employers. Am I correct?
I do not know that the hon. gentleman can draw that inference ; my remarks I think do not necessarily imply that.	.	'
I think when we are voting large sums of money for the purpose of conciliation, we should know from the minister upon what principle we proceed.
Everything depends on the 'Circumstances of each case.

There is nothing to be ashamed of. There are many very worthy citizens adverse to the recognition of the unions, and on the other hand there is a large body of people who think that it is the proper principle to follow. But I think we are entitled to'some expression of opinion from the Department of Labour. The hon. gentleman ought to be an expert on this subject.

Possibly I might make my views still clearer if I were to say that when I have actively intervened in the settlement of strikes, in some cases I have tried to get the employers to see the wisdom of recognizing the union. But everything depends on the circumstances of the case'; it is not possible to lay down a general rule.

I have in mind a case in which the minister might set an excellent example to employers generally, that is, to use his influence on the government of which he is a member to recognize the union whenever circumstances of employment offered by that government makes it possible. This afternoon, for instance, an hon. member asked about the union label, and why it appeared upon the ' Labour Gazette.' The answer, as I understand it, was that the minister did not know how it came to appear, but he thought it appeared, there because conditions in the government Printing Bureau were satisfactory to the labour unions. It seems to me, under the circumstances, that there is another reason, and that is that the ' Gazette ' is not printed at the government Bureau at all, but is, as the minister stated before recess, sent outside to an office which is a union office, which does recognize the union, and is, therefore, entitled to use the union label which appears there.

The ' Labour Gazette,' I understand, was at the outset printed in the Printing Bureau, then the Bureau became too 'crowded with work, and decided to have it printed outside. But the ' Gazette ' used the union label from the outset.

Now that we learn from the minister that this union label was attached to the ' Labour Gazette ' when it was printed at the Printing Bureau, I might ask if it is not permissible to put the union label on all government work? If it is not permissible Mr. KING.
for instance, to put it on this volume of estimates, and upon all government work? Now, it occurs to me that if the minister would follow out his idea already stated in this House, that the government should be a model employer of labour, here is an excellent chance to set a good example, and to show to employers generally that this model employer of labour, the government, recognizes the work of the labour unions, far as I can see, in acknowledging the in the interest of workingmen generally, and that in token of that recognition, the department desires the union label to be placed upon all printing emanating from the government printing office. We have already been told that conditions there are entirely satisfactory to the union, so there can be no great difficulty involved, as far as I can see, in acknowledging the union, since the conditions have been made entirely satisfactory to them. I would ask the minister whether it would not have a great effect upon other employers, and be an encouragement to them to concede this point to their men, and if the minister will use his influence with the government of which he is a member to have the printers' union acknowledged in connection with the government printing, and put the union label on all works issued from the government Bureau. I would like to ask the minister whether he has ever taken that up with his colleagues, and whether or not he thinks the government should have the union label represented on all government printing?

I recognize that there are a good many views in the country as to the propriety of using the union label. It might be that to use the union label on the ' Labour Gazette ' would be about as far as we'can go at present, in view of the differences of opinion prevailing on that subject.
That is not answering the question.

I think it is answering the question so far as the minister cares to go on record. But it is unsatisfactory to those who believe in the recognition of the unions. I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman that he takes a great responsibility in the course he is pursuing, because he stands directly behind the employer who refuses to recognize the union, and therefore makes it impossible to have the conciliation which the department is organized to secure.

It looks to me as though the Minister of Laboui is working for the employer instead of Ihe men. That has been instanced in cases before this. In those strikes down east, as far as I can judge from the newspapers, the minister stood by the employer to the

injury of the man. The men always seemed to come out second best. The same thing applies to the Grand Trunk strike. In that case the minister wanted to show the employees of the Grand Trunk what a great thing he was doing for them, and the impression that went all through the country was that the interest of the men had been served by the minister, that they were all to be reinstated, that everything was to be lovely, and that the Grand Trunk had been brought to time. But you see from the reports afterwards that it turns out the very opposite; the men are the ones that are turned down. As I understood, the Department of Labour was formed for the protection of tire men. It was always understood that the employers could look after themselves, but it was the men that this Department of Labour was being organized for. In all these great strikes that have occurred for some years the whole difficulty, as I understood it from hon. gentlemen in this House, and from ministers when they wanted to organize this great Labour Department, was that the men had not any protection, and that if we had a Minister of Labour there would be no trouble at all because he could always force the employer to come to terms. I was certainly led to believe that, and if I had not been so led to believe it I would not have agreed to this large expenditure each year. It was only going to be $7,000 or $8,000 when it started, but I venture to say that in a year or two it will be rolled up, like that of the Department of Militia, while the Department of Agriculture will be allowed to remain as it is. The Minister of Labour cannot prove to this House one instance where he has helped the men out, the very thing that he was expected to do when he was put in that position. In every case he has gone to the employer, made a deal with him, and the men have always come out second best. I would like to ask the Minister of Labour what he considers to be the duty of the department in cases of this kind. Is the department therefor the purpose of assisting the men, working particularly in the interests of the men to prevent strikes, and get them reinstated in case of a strike, or is the department there for the sole purpose of taking the side of the employer to the detriment of the men?

I do not think it the duty of the Department of Labour to champion the case of either side. The position of the Department of Labour is the same as that of any other department of the government, the duty being to consider the general good of the community, and to see that justice is done in every way possible as between employers and employees. I think that is all the working classes expect of any one acting on their behalf expect. They do not want coddling or protecting. All
they are asking is that the government
shall see that there is fair nlay and that is what the Department of Labour has endeavoured to secure.

That is what I think the Department of Labour should be for. At the same time the weak side is that of the men because the employers have capital and can stop the fight. The men have no capital and the minute a strike takes place they have no protection. They must have something to keep their families and they are the weak side. If any help is to be given, the men should get help from the department. Why I mention this is that in so far as I can see in any strikes that I have read about as being settled, the whole trouble is that the employer has got the better of the men. For instance, take the Grand Trunk strike; if you travel by the Grand Trunk to-day you will find that the men are not all put back, and the minister certainly will not deny this statement. He assured the public that every man was to be taken back, and that within three months. If there is any doubt about that I would like the minister to say so now. Was not that the understanding? He was trying to let the men understand that he had done them a great service, but the result is that the men were not taken back as he led them to believe they would be, and they are not back today. Whenever the Department of Labour, over which he presides, do take any part, they certainly should see to it that whatever arrangement they make is carried out. They did not in that ease and they did not in the case of the strikes down in Nova Scotia. In those cases they did not act properly in so far as the men were concerned. I would like the minister now to give me one case where the men were all taken back, put in their positions just as they were before, perfectly satisfied, and that the minister has done what was right in so far as they were concerned.

I should like, in answering my hon. friend, to let the statements of the workingmen speak for themselves rather than that I should speak on behalf of the department. I read to the House the otheT evening the expressions of opinion given by the leaders of the Grand Trunk strike as to the service that had been rendered by the Department of Labour, and if my hon. friend would like to hear these opinions again I should be very glad to repeat them.
I would like to hear who the leaders are.

There was a communication from Mr. A. B. Garretson, president of the Brotherhood of Railway Conductors, one of the organizations involved in the strike. On the 10th August I received the following letter.
August when?
1910. The strike was settled on the 2nd of August.
Yes, that is right.

Cedar Rapids, Iowa,
August 10,1910.

Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,-I take this opportunity of expressing to you on behalf of not only myself and my associate officers, but of the organization at large and the more especially the Canadian membership thereof, the profound obligation under which we lie for the services of yourself and your associate minister in connection with the settlement of the strike upon the Grand Trunk and the Central Vermont railways. The ready recognition by you of the justification for the claims of the men on those properties and the exercise of personal and governmental influence toward securing a termination of the strike on those properties will not be forgotten by our membership and I sincerely trust that those most directly affected, namely, our Canadian citizens, will, in the future, make that appreciation thoroughly apparent.
In conclusion, kindly accept my expressions of highest personal regard, and believe me, Sincerely and gratefully yours, (Signed) A. B. GARRETSON, President.
Did you ever hear from him again?

Yes, I have had other communications from him. Then, there have been other communications in magazines published by these organizations much of the same nature. I have here a pamphlet issued by Mr. W. G. Lee, president of the Railroad Trainmen, the other organization involved in this strike. At page 10 of this pamphlet, wljich is issued to the members of the organization, Mr. Lee states:
The ministers of the Crown and particularly the hou. W. L. Mackenzie King, Minister of Labour, and Sir Frederick Borden, Minister of Militia, were largely instrumental in bringing about a settlement of the strike. They kept in close touch with the strike, throughout its duration and made the most of every opportunity to bring the two parties together. They are due high praise for their interest in the welfare of the striking employees and of those affected hy the interruption of the company's traffic. Their efforts on behalf of the men are appreciated hy both organizations and by officers and individual n embers of the brotherhood.
There have been several other communications of a like kind, received from members of both organizations, and the men themselves, I may say, have taken strong exception to the endeavour on the part of Mr. KING.
some, to hold the government responsible for any delinquency on the part of the Grand Trunk company in carrying out in all particulars, as they understand, the terms of the agreement. The position of the parties in regard to that strike was this. The government intervened with a view of helping to terminate the strike, the strike was terminated through government intervention, by an agreement signed by each of the two parties. That agreement was brought about through the good offices Of the government. The carrying out of the terms of that agreement is a matter of contract between the parties, and if the agreement has not been carried out in the manner which some would like to have seen it, it is in no way the fault of the government, but rather a delinquency on the part of one of the parties in carrying out the obligation which they have signed. That is the view taken by the men themselves.

I shall not speak at length as this matter will come before the House in another form, but I desire to make two or three further statements to complement what the minister has stated. Without in the slightest, contradicting the minister's statement that he received some communication of a eulogistic nature about the 10th of August. He was not so good however, as to read some later communication from the same gentlemen or from equally high leaders of the workmen, that if something was not done and done speedily, they would put the men back in the same position as before the 10th of August, and the men claim they were betrayed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. King).
I challenge the hon. gentleman to point out where any workingman has charged that he was betrayed by the Minister of Labour.
I am talking of leaders of the strike.
I challenge him to produce any communication to that effect.

I shall be very happy at the stage to which I have referred to bring down the letters. If the minister looks through his correspondence, he will find a letter from one of these leaders, written months after the 10th of August, in which that leader finding fault with the way in which the agreement was carried out, says they would put the men back where they weTe before the 10th of August. I will undertake to produce such a letter. The minister spoke of the desire of the government to see justice done. That is what the men complain, that the government were so anxious to sit by and see justice done, that they did nothing to compel it to be done. The minister says that there

was an agreement between the men and the Grand Trunk by which the strike was settled. Is that statement the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth ? Does he -not know that when the agreement was made, the men objected to having such indefinite words in it, as that they would be taken back ' as soon as possible '; they refused -to accept the agreement with these indefinite terms, because the expression might mean the day of judgment. The men left the conference, -and subsequently the minister of labour notified the men tha/t the Grand Trunk company had given as an interpretation of the words ' as soon as possible,' at the outside, 90 days. On the strength of that notification that agreement read that they would be put back within 90 days and the strike was called off. I would ask the minister if, fr-om the day he notified -the men that they would be put back in 90 days, he did a single thing to see that that agreement was carried out ? He read a letter to the House in w'hich Mr. Hays repudiated the agreement, and said there was no undertaking to put the men back in 90 days, that the Grand Trunk must be the sole judges of who were proper men to be in their employ. The Grand Trunk wilfully violated the agreement. These men appealed to the Minister of Labour and if ever there was a time when a powerful minister, with a desire to do justice to labour, had the opportunity to do so, that was the time. Surely all the minister had to do with the Grand Trunk, which is so intertwined with the affairs of this country, was to say: I was a party to that agreement, Sir Frederick Borden and I were present when the agreement was made, the men were not there at all, but you made a promise, and I, acting in good faith von your promise, had the strike called off; now we insist on the Grand Trunk standing by the agreement. If the minister for once had ventured to address the corporation, which many people consider the master of the government, in those terms, there is not the slightest doubt in the world that the unfortunate men, who, evidently wrongfully, since many of them have since been reinstated, were deprived of their positions, would have been put back within 90 days. Therefore, the minister can hardly claim th-at he was acting impartially between the two parties to that agreement. The agreement was wilfully violated by the president of the Grand Trunk, it was not a case of conflict of evidence; the minister has the agreement and the letter, both signed by Charles M. Hays, as diametrically contradictory as any two statements could be. It would not have been hard for the minister to say to Mr. Hays:	You may say one thing at one
time, and another at another time to some people, but so far -as this government is
concerned, when you make a bargain with us, you have to keep it. Instead of that; the minister did not say a single word for the men, but he wrote to them, saying that he was no party to the agreement, only a witness thereto, and the best advice he could give them was, that Mr. Hays had the power in his hand, and perhaps the best thing they could do, was to -accept the situation as it was. Surely in the fact of that, the minister can hardly claim that he did all he could to do justice to the labouring men.

I do not desire to go into a discussion of the Grand Trunk strike. The contract was signed between the parties. It is quite true, as my hon. friend has said, the Grand Trunk Company stated that by ' as soon as possible ' would be meant not more than 90 days. That was not put in writing at the time, as one of the parties to the contract did not wish to have anything stated on that point one way or the other, and the other party, by way of compromise, gave it as their view that they would be satisfied if an assurance were given in a form which could be vouched for, and on that consideration they would not insist on it going into the contract. The assurance was given that by ' as soon as possible ' was meant 90 days. That part has never been disputed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, as I understand. If it had been I would have stated here that that was the assurance and I have always stood prepared to say that it was. The difficulty that has arisen, as I understand, is over the interpretation which the company has put upon the words ' found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct.' The company claim that the men who have not been taken back have been guilty of disorderly conduct. If some men have not been reinstated who should have been, the responsibility is on the company for the manner in which they have interpreted that part of the contract. Personally, I think the company has taken a very narrow view of its obligations under this contract, and I have not hesitated to say so very frankly to the company. As the hon. gentleman knows, Judge Barron is at the present time inquiring into the cases of the men who were not taken back. He is doing that at the instance of the Grand Trunk as a result of the pressure brought to bear on the company by the government for that purpose, and if any of these men have been reinstated since who were not taken back at the end of the ninety days, it is the result of that pressure. The government has all along insisted that the company should interpret this clause in as generous a way as it is possible to do.

The minister has just stated in as many words that in as much


as Judge Barron is adjudicating on these cases under the pay of the Grand Trunk company, so far as that is concerned, he sits, not as a judge of any Canadian court, but as a Grand Trunk employee.

I think Judge Barron's own letter in reply to the request of the Grand Trunk Company to investigate these cases is, perhaps, the best answer that can be given to my bon. friend. Judge Barron said that he w'ould not accept the position unless he were allowed an absolutely free hand to decide the cases on their merits, and I am told by the leaders of some of the men who appeared before Judge Barron that they feel perfectly satisfied with the manner in which he is conducting the investigation, and will have full confidence in the justice of his findings. If I understand my hon. friend rightly, he is endeavouring to hold the government responsible for the non-reinstatement of some of these employees.
Certainly. The government acted for them, and did not get them back.

I would point out to my hon. friend that these men do not take the position of my hon. friend with regard to the carrying out oi this obligation, but take the only position which any one looking at the matter with absolute impartiality will take, namely, that if there has been any failure in carrying out the terms of the contract, the party who is responsible for that failure is the delinquent. I have a letter from Mr. Murdock, vicepresident of the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen, addressed to myself, and inclosing a copy of an answer which was sent to my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). I am sorry he is not in his seat at the moment, because I rather hesitate to read a communication which introduces his name in his absence. But the letter sent to me is a formal letter, and after receiving it I took care to inquire whether it was a public communication, and was informed that it was, and, as it answers my hon. friend, I will venture to read it to the committee. The hon. member for South Simcoe asked me in the House the other day some questions which I answered categorically. It appears that my hon. friend had communicated with both the representative of the trainmen and the representative of the conductors, submitting the same questions to them, and asking for their views in reply. When he did so these gentlemen communicated with me, as they have done all through, informing me of their action and of the communications which they have received. The . letter to * me is as follows:

I do not think the minister has proved that he has succeeded yet in making any settlement which has been in the interests of the men. Of course, Mr. Murdock knows well that it would never do to quarrel with the Minister of Labour, because he is the only one who could help the men out, and for that reason the men called him in. The Minister went down and made that settlement on behalf of the men, and the minister knows that if he had not given his word, and if the men had not felt that they had the government at their back, they never would have had agreed to that settlement.
What then would have happened?

The men would have stayed out a week or two longer and the Grand Trunk railway would have had to come to time. There can be no question about that. The people along the line would not stand it. My hon. friend knows that if he had not got a settlement made, there were important men on his own side of the House who could have brought such a pressure on him that he would have been forced to make a settlement. The whole country was in an uproar over this strike, and the Grand Trunk railway would

have been forced to settle it within a week or two, in any event, and so they got the Minister of Labour to come to their rescue.
The hon. gentleman cannot show that from the correspondence.
I have read what was in the newspapers at the time.

I am afraid my hon. friend has been reading the wrong papers. If he will take the facts as they are, he will see that a telegram was sent to me at Ottawa by Mr. Murdock asking me to go to Montreal to intervene. In that telegram it was distinctly stated that Mr. Garretson and Mr. Lee had been endeavouring to get an interview with Mr. Hays but found it impossible, and they asked me to come down and do my best to obtain a settlement. In this connection I would like to correct what I said the other evening. I then said that Mr. Murdock and Mr. Berry had tried to get a conference with Mr. Hays before Mr. Garretson and Mr. Lee had a conference with him. In that I was wrong. Mr. Murdock and Mr. Berry had not had any conference with Mr. Hays. The parties were apart, the difficulty was to get them together, and Messrs. Garretson and Lee came to this country to obtain an interview with Mr. Hays and see if they could not terminate the difficulty. It was when they found they could not succeed in doing this that the Canadian leaders sent a telegram to Ottawa asking me to intervene. It was, therefore, only at the request of the men that I went to Montreal, because I had no communication with the company whatever. In fact my chief difficulty was to get the company to allow me to intervene; and were it not for the assistance of my hon. colleague the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) it might have been impossible for me to get even that opportunity.
That was probably at the first, but not later, because later on the Grand Trunk railway wanted the strike settled.

The company never wanted it settled. So far as the Grand Trunk railway were concerned, it was impossible for me to understand their position. I believe they' were prepared to keep up the strike for a month, even if thereby they should ruin the whole concern. That was the difficulty in bringing about a settlement. The Grand Trunk railway wished to effectively defeat the men and their organization if it were at all possible to do it.
No doubt that was the case until the president of the Grand Trunk railway started for Canada.
The president of the Grand Trunk railway?
I mean the chairman of the Grand Trunk railway in England. The strike was settled about two days before he landed in New York.

Throughout the whole trouble the difficulty was to get the Grand Trunk railway to settle at all, and it was only after the greatest possible pressure that the company was brought to consent to a settlement in the end. I have no hesitation in saying that Mr. Hays, had he not been forced to feel that he owed some obligation to the country, would have kept up that, strike until he had succeeded in worsting both organizations, even if he destroyed the property of the company in so doing.

I admit that such was the case until within a week or so before the strike was settled. But the position of the company then compelled it to settle. With its securities going down in England, it could not have allowed that strike to continue much longer. Supposing we take it for granted that the minister went down on behalf of the men, the men trusted him, theyf placed their case absolutely in his hands, and they felt they had the government at their bach when the minister made that settlement.
And they were perfectly satisfied.

Yes, because they expected that the settlement which the minister had made would be carried out, but they were afterwards sadly disappointed. The minister knows that the company is not carrying it out. At the end of the 90 days, very few men were taken back, and those who were taken back were not reinstated in their former positions, and are not in those positions to-day. They are on the road but not in such good positions. What I cannot understand is tbis. The Minister of Labour knows that the labouring men look to him in his official position to see to their interests. It was in their interests mainly that the labour department was established. Great corporations, of course, have occasionally difficulties with their men and the men look to the Department of Labour to help them in these difficulties. The minister settled this strike, and the men relied on the company living up to the terms of the settlement. In this they have been disappointed and there is now no possible way of their grievances being removed and their difficulties straightened out because once they have gone back you can hardly expect them to strike again. The result is a great deal of suffering to-day among a number of the Grand Trunk railway employees due to

the fact that the Minister of Labour did not see that the agreement was carried out to the letter.
And how much suffering does the hon. gentleman think there would have been if the strike had not been settled ?

There would not have been another week's trouble, and the men would all have been taken back.
Mr. {1ESBITT. Who says so ?
I say so. And the hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt) himself knows that it would have been settled in another week.

The hon. member has a right to his opinion. But from the information that I got along the line, I believe the Grand Trunk would have settled the strike in a very short time But the question I asked the minister at the start, was whether he could name an instance of a strike being settled by him in a way satisfactory to the men and the employers. He mentioned this Grand Trunk case, and I think that the discussion shows that that settlement was not satisfactory. If this is the only case he can name, I cannot see much use for the department.

I have here the issue of September 10, last of the official monthly publication of the. Brotherhod of Railroad Trainmen. It gives a statement of this case from the point of view of the men themselves. At page 797,- the following appears:
The company, however, was able to secure enough _ strike breakers to enable it to run 148 freight trains within the twenty-four hours ending at 6 p.m., August 2, handling an average of twenty-two cars per train" While this avei-age of trains run was far below normal conditions, a start had been made in the freight service, and it was only a question of time when the entire service would be resumed.
There is the statement as to the freight situation. This publication goes on:
Passenger service on the main line was but slightly impaired at any time during the strike, while the branch passenger line service was demoralized for about a week.
I think that statement is absolutely correct-that it was only a question of time. But, in my opinion, it would have been a
long time. Meantime, the country would have suffered irreparable loss and injury,
to say nothing of the possible loss of life and the loss of property to individuals, and certainly whatever the outcome the men would have fared pretty badly.
Who wrote that article ?

This is called ' The Railroad Trainman,' and it is published monthly at Cleveland, Ohio, by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen. T. L. Cease is given as editor and manager. This is the official publication of the Brotherhood interested in this strike. The men who were most concerned and who had first-hand knowledge of the facts, recognized the service rendered in terminating that strike, and getting a contract which secured the reinstatement of the men, with the exception of the few who are still out. I think the number involved was about 4,500, while the number still out, are in the vicinity, I understand, of 200. What was secured was an agreement that they should go back into the company's employment, and it may be that even those who are still out will be returned to the service. I hope they will. Their representative states, under date February 20:
The agreement made when the strike was called off was, under ihe circumstances, equitable and amply sufficient to conserve the rights and interests of all concerned, public, employer and employee.
If there has been any difficulty since, the parties who are responsible, and who are being held responsible by the men, are the Grand Trunk officials, who have not played, perhaps, as generous a part as I think the country would, on the whole, have expected them to play. I am free to say that if I had been manager of the Grand Trunk I would have acted in a very different manner from the way in which the Grand Trunk has acted. But one must concede that, every man has a right to manage his own business as he thinks best, and must be responsible for the outcome.

The difference between my hon. friend (Mr. Reid, Grenville) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. King), seems to narrow down to a. small point. This letter from Mr. Murdock proves, what everybody knew, that the settlement made between the men and the Grand Trunk, as a settlement, was satisfactory. The representatives of the men had done their duty, and we assume that Mr. Hays had done his duty, acting for the Grand Trunk,
And has the government done its duty ?

I was just coming to-that. The government intervened at that

time to give a definition of three or four words, and the strike was called off solely by virtue of the definition of the words given by the government. The whole difficulty since has arisen over the interpretation-

No, my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) is mistaken. The government's part in the work was really getting these parties to meet. That was the great difficulty. Mr. Hays took the position-that there should be no dealing between them, and the men had tried to get an interview and could not. It took a good deal of persuasion to bring about an interview in the_ first instance. And when the interview did take place, it took a good deal more persuasion to prevent the parties flying off at a tangent and making matters practically worse than before. For three or four days, it took as strenuous work, I believe, as any two men could perform, and as much patience as a man could possess, to keep these two parties together and hold them together, despite the feeling between .them, until a contract was drawn up which each was prepared to sign. That was the service of the government, and it was rendered, according to statements of the company and the men alike, in such a way as to bring about a contract which was' absolutely equitable and fair.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. King) does not wish the House to understand that the government dictated the terms of the settlement. The settlement, I take it, was come to between the men and the Grand Trunk, however they were brought together.

That agreement was made between the men and the Grand Trunk, however they were brought together, and that agreement has caused no difficulty since, with the exception of the unfortunate words which were entrusted to the care of the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Militia and Defence.* Over those words the whole difficulty has arisen.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. There has been absolutely no difficulty over those words-the words he refers to, I suppose, are ' as soon as possible.' The words ' as soon as possible ' have in themselves no definite meaning whatever. The men wished to have ' immediately ' put in; the company wished to have the words ' as soon as possible ' left, leaving the meaning indefinite. The Minister of Militia and myself said to the company: Put some meaning on these words; you have no right to say you mean ' as soon as possible ' unless you are prepared to give some definite time. Do you mean to take those men back within a stated time, or not to put them back at all? If you mean a stated time, name the time. We had great difficulty in getting them to name a time, and finally ninety days was agreed upon. Then the question came up. Should the ninety days go into the contract? The company did not wish ninety days to be put in writing, because at the time they did not wish it to appear to the public that they had settled this strike and agreed to take every man back at the end of ninety days. Now if they had taken every man back, this agreement about the ninety days would never have been formally disclosed. It was understood by all parties that nothing should be said about that, provided they lived up to it. The company does not deny that, they admit they promised to take these men. hack within ninety days, they say now they have taken them back, and the point of difference is, not the ninety days, but it is one of the terms of the contract which says * Except those who have been guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct.' These words were not the words of the Minister of Militia and myself, they were the words agreed upon between the parties themselves, and it is over these words that they are differing to-day. The company says these 200 men have been guilty of disorderly conduct, the men say they have not, and it is over these words that the difficulty has taken place. So my hon. friend is wrong when he says it is over the words ' as soon as possible ' that all the trouble has arisen.

I would just ask the minister to take the trouble to read the cor-

respondence, and he will find there, over Mr. Hayes' signature, the statement that the reason they have not taken the men back was because the Grand Trunk Company must be the judge of the competency and fitness of the men, and they have a right to discharge their men on the Grand Trunk system regardless of whether they had already been there before. It shows a new factor introduced by Mr. Hayes, which was not in the agreement, and which new factor is the cause of all the trouble and dissatisfaction which have since arisen.
If it is a new factor introduced by Mr. Hayes which all the trouble is about, then it could not be anything which the Minister of Militia and myself are responsible for.
I understand by what was said by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) that Judge Barron was in the -pay of the Grand Trunk Company. I would like to know if that is a fact?
Judge Barron has been appointed by the Grand Trunk Company to investigate the cases of all the men who have not been reinstated, or not been taken back.
Is he in the pay of the Grand Trunk Company? '
I do not presume he is acting for nothing, I presume the Grand Trunk are paying for his services.
Does not the minister know whether he is being paid or not by the Grand Trunk?

I cannot say what the consideration is. All I know is that Judge Barron sent me a communication himself stating that he h,ad been asked by the Grand Trunk Railway Company to investigate the cases of these men. In the first instance, I suggested, when this difficulty arose as to the non re-instatement of certain men on the ground that they had been guilty of acts of violence, that the matter should be referred to some third party, and I suggested Judge Barron's name, as he had been engaged on similar difficulties before. He had acted as chairman of the board which prevented a strike of the street railway men in Toronto, and I knew him to be acceptable to the employees, and being a judge, I thought he was the right kind of a man to act, I suggested that he would be a good person. The company would not accept him from the outset, and as I have indicated tc my hon. friend, the government intimated to the company pretty firmly that the cases of these men ought to be looked into, that they ought to take a generous view, or what the public would
regard as a fair view. Then the company asked Judge Barron to investigate. I have here a letter which was written on December 23, by J. G. O'Donogahue to Judge Barron, which has reference to the view the men take of his appointment:
I had a talk with Messrs. Murdock and Berry this morning and as a result I take the responsibility of saying to you to go ahead with the suggestions of yesterday.
That had reference to the judge investigating without solicitors for either side; he preferred to investigate the matter himself.
Their view is that as they were ready to accept you as a government nominee they will have just as much confidence in you in the other capacity.
I am told that the men have absolute confidence in Judge Barron's ability and integrity and in the justice of his decision, whatever it may be.

My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Crosby), before the committee rose at six o'clock, was discussing with the Minister of Labour the question of the recognition of the unions in the province of Nova Scotia growing out of the difficulties in the coal mining districts for the last year or two. I would ask him if it is a fact that out of the nineteen hundred odd unions that were in existence in Canada in 1909, over ninety per cent of these were international unions?
I can hardly say offhand whether there are ninety per cent, but I would say that certainly a preponderating majority were international unions?
I think I remember the minister saying that out of 1,900 odd there were 1,900 international unions, which would be really over ninety per cent.

I might point out that the membership in these unions varies considerably. One union might have a hundred members, and ten other unions together would have no more than a hundred members. Therefore, the mere number of the unions would not signify much.

I am informed it is a fact that about 1,900 of the nearly 2,000 unions in the Dominion of Canada are international unions. Now, I would ask the minister if it is not a fact that the question of the recognition of the United Mine Workers' of America was involved on three different occasions when boards of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Act were constituted in the province of Nova Scotia, and that each of these boards was constituted by an appointee of the men who are compelled to appoint a representative when they make their application, and that the other two appointees on each of these three occasions, were appointees of

the governments. The first one of these investigations which took place was after the application was received by the Department of Labour on the 4th March, 1909, and the constitution of the board was made up of his Honour W. B. Wallace, county court judge of Halifax county, chairman, appointed by the minister in the absence of any joint recommendation of the other members of the board, and Mr. G. S. Campbell, Halifax, Nova Scotia, appointed by the minister in the absepce of a recommendation by the employing company. In that case two members of the board were appointed by the minister. The question of the recognition of a uniop is largely an economic question, and it seems to me that the minister in selecting two representatives to.form the personnel of this board might very well have selected some one familiar with economics, some professor of economics in one of our universities. Professor Shortt, who served on 28 or 29 boards of conciliation, would have made an ideal chairman of one of these boards. I discovered in 1907 that Professor Shortt is a strong advocate of international unions, a firm believer in trade combines and that he believes that a healthy restriction on trade combines is international union. It might be that other economists in this country share the views of that distinguished gentleman. However, on the occasion of which I speak, the chairman of the board was the Hon. Mr. Justice Wallace, county court judge of Halifax. I do not know anything about his capacity to sit in judgment on a question of economics, but, as a member of his profession, and in his capacity as a judge,
I am sure that he has the confidence of all people who come in contact with him. But, to sit in judgment in an inquiry as to whether or not a trade union should be recognized I do not recognize his Honour Mr. Justice Wallace as a competent authority. A great deal of prejudice was exercised against international unionism in the province of Nova Scotia at that time. Evidently members of these boards forgot or took no cognizance of the fact that the principal industries of that province are developed by international capital. We have one coal mine in the province of Nova Scotia controlled by a company whose whole directorate, almost to a man, are American citizens, whose head office is in Boston and whose annual meetings are held there. I have reference to the Acadia Coal Company. The investment of American capital in the coal mining industries of our country means American boards of directors and means, as in this particular case to which I have reference, American mine managers, American overmen, American underground managers, American superintendents, or in other words, American bosses. The other appointee of the Mr. MADDIN.
government on the first board of conciliation which was held on these matters between the Dominion Coal Company and their employees was Mr. G. S. Campbell, of Halifax. Mr. Campbell is an employer of labour, a square, upright citizen in every respect as I know him to be, but still an employer of labour and you would naturally have expected that the Industrial Disputes Act, which says that any one having an interest in the case shall not sit on the board, would have guided the minister in judging whether or not an employer of labour would be an unbiased member of a board of conciliation, and would have led him to the conclusion that, being an employer of labour, he was unfitted to discharge his duties impartially. That is one case where the government appointed two members of the board. That was the first case that came up. The next one was the dispute between the employees of the Nova Scotia Steel & Coal Company and the United Mine Workers' of America. In both those instances the United Mine Workers' had named as their nominee the president of their organization. Now, I quite admit that Mr. Campbell as an employer of labour was in as good a position to render a fair and equitable judgment as the president of the organization was on the board, and I condemn his appointment to sit on the board in the same manner that I would condemn the appointment of Mr. Campbell. But I am dealing now with the appointees of the government. Mr. Campbell was appointed in the Dominion Coal Company's matter, and at Sydney Mines the personnel of the board was made up of these gentlemen :	His
Honour Judge Chipman, Kentville, N.S , chairman, appointed by the minister ; His Honour Judge A. McGillivray, Antigonish, N.S., appointed by the Minister and Mr. McDougall again representing the employees. His Honour * Mr. Justice Chipman is, in so., far as I know, just such a gentleman as the chairman of the board that sat in the dispute on the 4th March in which the Dominion Coal Company and its employers were concerned. As to. his previous record with regard to organized labour I have no information, but the minister could have found the record of His Honour Mr. Justice McGillivray with regard to organized labour, and I think il he had made himself acquainted with that gentleman's past record in connection with labour unions, if he had known the active part that Mr. Justice McGillivray had taken in the legislature of Nova Scotia against organized labour in any shape or form, he might well have hesitated before he would have asked him to sit in judgment as a representative of the employer to determine a question between the employer and the employee with regard to the recognition of the labour union. In

1878 the Provincial Workmen's Association in Nova Beotia sought incorporation under the laws of the province. His Honour Mr. Justice McGillivray was a member of the government of Nova 'Scotia at that day, and he it was who led the attack against the organization. The government refused to pass an Act incorporating the Provincial Workmen's Association. In 1882 the Grand Council of the Provincial Workmen's Association sought incorporation in Nova Scotia again and when the Attorney General Mr. C. J. Town-shend introduced the measure Mr. McGillivray said that :
Mr. McGillivray thought it was a very peculiar Bill and one that required some consideration before being passed, and that it would be imprudent to deal with it until first its real object had been ascertained. There was nothing to show what the purpose of the association sought to be incorporated was, except that it was to promote the moral, material, social, and physical well-being of its members and to manage their pecuniary aftairs. Now under so indefinite a purpose much harm might be concealed. The House had nothing to do with associations of the kind proposed, and it would not be wise to make a precedent. He, therefore, would move that the Bill be read this day three months.
On the second occasion on which the Provincial Workmen's Association made an effort to get their association incorporated in Nova Scotia, Mr. Justice McGillivray, then a member of the opposition, moved the three months' hoist of the Bill and he urged that further particulars should be brought to the attention of the House, and that the constitution of this organization and its by-laws should be submitted to the House.
On a later day the Attorney General brought the Bill up again.
Hon. Mr. Townshend said in reference to !he Bill to incorporate the Provincial Workmen's Association which had excited considerable discussion in committee on Friday last, in accordance with the wish expressed by the House at that time he had communicated with the secretary of that association and obtained from him several copies of the constitution and by-laws and also a statement of the object of the association.
The secretary of the association at that time was the Hon. Robert Drummond, now editor and publisher of the ' Maritime Mining Record ' in Nova Scotia, and one of the leading authorities on coal mining in that province.
In his reply the secretary said: I send you a number of constitutions of our society. I think you will find them as good a code of laws as in any society. The objects of the society are therein defined as being to strive by every legitimate means to improve the condition material, social and moral-of our members. Our association has done much good and is stimulating the workingmen who
come under its influence to better their con-diton; to first of all respect themselves, as the surest way of gaining the respect of others. We seek to get the best remuneration possible for our labour, but we inculcate that high wages are nothing without an exercise of prudence and economy. We are, if you will, a trades union on an improved principle and allowed by law. See chap. 165, Rev. Stat. sec. 2, (appendix).
This was read by the Attorney General, and then the Bill finally came up for discussion before the House, and Mr. McGillivray, from his place in the House, said:
Mr. McGillivray suggested that as there were several hon. gentlemen absent when this bill was discussed on a previous day it would be better to let it lie over and take up some other Bills.
It is to be observed that Mr. McGillivray did everything he could to delay the passage of the Bill, or even its discussion. However, the matter came up for discussion, and then he said:
Mr. McGillivray did not oppose the Bill for any other purpose than that of getting the fullest understanding of what it contemplated.
The purpose for which this society sought to be incorporated were not very clearly set ferth. The first object stated was that of n an aging the pecuniary affairs of the society. These were words of very extensive meaning, and very dangerous powers might be gnen by the use of these general and indefinite terms. The Bill proposed to incorporate the grand council and all the subordinate lodges. Some of those lodges were not in this province but in New Brunswick and the House was asked to pass upon by-laws of aa institution not only belonging to this province but New Brunswick as well. One of the objects of the association, as explained in the constitution, was to shorten the hours of labour and to strive to obtain legislation by which the more efficient management of the mines might be effected, and to enforce the legislation already existing. Now it was well known that the labourers in this country were not overworked. Their hours particularly in the coal mines were not long and they were well paid except when the times we re hard and all concerned were obliged to suffer and the wages were reduced in proportion. Then with respect to the management of the mines there was already an Act on. the statute-book during the passing of which representatives of this association were heard and every amendment that they asked for had been substantially incorporated in the Act. Why then incorporate this society and give it a legal status when the constitution of the society was so vague' and would perhaps give them power to pass by-laws by which the trade of the country would be t ampered. Trades' unions were dangerous things. In other countries where the miners were subjected to oppression there might be some call for them, but there was no such oppression exercised in this country and the miners were fully protected by the law. These unions had promoted strikes which were very injurious not only to the employer-:

but in a greater measure still to the men themselves. In 1870 there was a strike in the United States of a serious character.
Mr. Chairman, under the new rules hon. gentlemen must talk to the question. I am sure that the strike the hon. gentleman is reading about in the United States has nothing to do with this question.
