speechtext:
If a point of order is raised, the item before the chair is
Conciliation and labour, including publication, printing, binding and distribution of the ' Labour Gazette,' and allowances to correspondents.
The first three words, ' conciliation and labour,' are so very broad in themselves that I hardly feel I can rule out any article that refers to such subjects.
So long as he confines himself to this country it is all right, but he is reading about a strike in the United States that has nothing to do with this country.
I think the hon. member must have been asleep and just woke up in the middle of my extract.
I was not asleep.

are the organizations of capital within the ranks of capitalists, and this is a good thing for employers as well as employees. Many of the best trades unions of this country discipline their men and thereby relieve their employers from a distasteful responsibility and harsh measures. Our labour unions to-day recognize that the man who shirks his work, the man who watches the clock, the man who arrives late at his machine or his work, is a drag on the union, and they either compel him to mend his ways or send him about his business. If a man trespasses on the rights of his employer and it comes to the knowledge of the union, the union takes that matter up and deals with him and thereby removes from the employer a disagreeable task. That is the condition which exists in the largest and strongest international unions, and I submit it would be better for capital in the province of Nova Scotia if some good substantial union, [DOT] be it international between Novg, Scotia and the United States or national in the sense that it would be affiliated with a union in Great Britain, existed in that province, because then capitalists would be able to deal with some good, strong substantial union which appreciated its responsibility, as a member of a powerful association, and would undertake to discipline its own men and thus bring about greater harmony than has heretofore existed in that turbulent industry-the coal industry of Nova Scotia. I am not making these observations, nor did I make those which I did two weeks ago in discussing this matter, for the purpose of harassing or delaying the passage of the minister's estimates. I have every sympathy with him in his administration of this new department which has embarked on legislation which is really of an experimental character; but he must realize that there are many imperfections in the Industrial Disputes Act, and in the Alien Labour Act that ought to be removed. I have no doubt that had my hon. friend read that article from the ' Trainman's Magazine ' a little further, he might have found that the main reason for the ability of the Grand Trunk railway to man their trains lay in the fact that they were able to hustle men across the line in spite of the Alien labour Act. No doubt the hon. minister has had complaints of the flagrant manner in which the Alien Labour Law has been violated even in the city of Ottawa; and so long as an employer can look upon this law simply as a joke, and bring in men from across the line whenever he likes, he need be under no apprehension on account of any labour union be it weak or strong. I have every sympathy with the minister in his undertaking this new portfolio, and instead of harassing him or annoying him in any way I would rather assist him in bringing to per-Mr. MADDIN.
fection some of these measures which are in the experimental stage. I ask him in all seriousness whether he does not think that some legislation should be enacted which would relieve the situation we have in Nova Scotia-a situation which enables an employer to say to his men:	I will
speak to you as individuals, as John Smith or Tom Brown, but not as members of this or the other union. If that condition be allowed to continue, there is no excuse for the existence of our Department of Labour. What I urge on the minister is that he should make it clear to employers of labour that they will be obliged to recognize a union regardless of where its affiliations or ties may bej and if he would do this, the difficulties under which the department labours would be substantially removed. For in that case he would have to deal with but two factors-the union and the company. But where there is no union he has to deal with individuals whose numbers may run up into the thousands as well as with the company. It is a physical impossibility to carry out the objects of the department unless there be a union. A couple of weeks ago I asked the hon. minister if he believed in trades unions and he said he, did. Then he must concede that the working man has the right to choose his own union and that the employer should not be permitted to say to him: You may join union A, but you must not join union B, for if you do I will either dismiss you or not hire you. If the hon. minister would seriously consider the framing of such legislation and also devise some means of enforcing the Alien Labour Law, and of constituting tribunals under the Industrial Disputes Act, I think he would make a very long step in advance, and would remove the cause of quite a number of breaches in the relations between labour and capital in this country.

I do not propose to follow my hon. friend throughout his meanderings or to discuss the labour question or trades unions or anything of that kind, but I rise simply to take objection to certain observations he made regarding Mr. Justice McGillivray. I happen to know Judge McGillivray, who was on the conciliation board referred to by my hon. friend, and I want to say that the remarks of the hon. gentleman, with regard to him are altogether uncalled for, and absolutely unjustified. To those who know Mr. Justice McGillivray these remarks would certainly sound very strange. The hon. gentleman has eulogized the United Mine Workers, but one must not forget that he has been the paid solicitor of that organization. He has had a brief from it within very recent time and for aught I know may still hold a retainer in its behalf. But great as may be the admiration

of my hon._ friend for the United Mine Workers, it is not regarded in Nova Scotia with at all that amount of respect. What I rose particularly for, however, was not to discuss this union, but to take objection to the remarks which my hon. friend made regarding Judge McGillivray. He intimated that Judge McGillivray was biased and partisan. Well, the hon. gentleman himself, if I remember rightly, served on a conciliation board; and I am sure no one will say, notwithstanding his advocacy of the United Mine Workers that when he sat on that board he did not exercise strict impartiality and discharge his duties without any prejudice. And I am quite sure that any one who knows Judge McGillivray and my hon. friend will have no hesitation whatever in saying that as great impartiality, justice and fairness should be expected from Judge McGillivray as from the hon. gentleman, and in saying this I am sure that I am casting no reflection on the latter but rather paying'him a compliment.
So far as the ability, integrity, impartiality and honesty of Judge McGillivray are concerned, words of mine are not needed. My hon. friend (Mr. Maddin) has, quoted some remarks made by Mr. McGillivray twenty-seven years ago, as he said, in opposition to a Bill intended for the amelioration of the condition of workingmen. The words as quoted must have struck hon. members as being such words as one would expect from a careful, impartial, truthful, judicial man like Judge McGillivray. He advised to go slow; he wanted to hear all sides. If I were disposed to offer advice, I would say that it would be well for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) to follow the lines pursued by Mr. McGillivray when he was in the legislature of Nova Scotia. But, admitting that Judge_ McGillivray was hostile to labour unions twenty-seven years ago, great changes may have since come over his mind. I can remember when the political views of the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) were entirely different from what they are to-day. That does not detract from his merits or involve any reflection upon them. Surely, even if Judge McGillivray did entertain views against labour organizations or unions-and there is no evidence that he did, mark you-the hon. gentleman might have been generous enough to believe that, in the course of twenty-seven years, his mind might have been changed and be disposed to see labour organizations in their proper light. But, when you consider the fact that Judge McGillivray was on the bench when he was on this arbitration, removed altogether from the turmoil of party warfare and freed from pred juice, and considering the fact also that he was sworn 135}
to discharge his duty impartially, to do what was right between man and man, I am sure the hon. member will agree with me, on reflection, that he spoke a little hastily when he insinuated that Judge McGillivray could not be depended upon to do justice between employer and employee. If I were interested, whether as employer or employee I would not have any hesitation in appealing to Judge McGillivray as an arbitrator who would give fair play and justice, in preference even to the hon. member for South Cape Breton, for whom I have the highest regard.

It seems to me that the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm) was unduly exercised about His Honour Mr. Justice McGillivray. I would utter a fervent ' amen ' to all the eulogies the hon. member cast upon the distinguished jurist. I merely pointed out that Mr. Justice McGillivray was an appointee of this government, one of six, but, notwithstanding that ninety per cent of the unions of this country were international unions, he and the other five recommended against the recognition of international unions. I pointed out that his past record in connection with unions was such as might cloud and w arp his judgment. Those were the terms I used. And I added that, doubtless, if such were the case, he was unconsciously biased. As a member of the legal profession, surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Chisholm) can understand a man possessing all the virtues that he attaches to Justice McGillivray could be unconsciously biased. The law takes cognizance of unconscious bias, and for that reason, forbids a father to try his son, a son to sit in judgment on his father, and others within certain grades of relationship to try their own kin. So far as Mr. Campbell and Mr. Archibald are concerned, I think they are, to say the least, the equal of Mr. Justice McGillivray in all the virtues assigned to him by the hon. member, and my observations with regard to these gentlemen were to show that their association, their training, the views they had expressed from time to time-views that there was no evidence to show had ever been changed-were such as to, perhaps, cloud and w^arp their judgment and thus render them unable to deal equitablv with a case of this kind. I imputed absolutely nothing dishonourable to any of the gentlemen whose names I have mentioned; I simply pointed out that, in preference to these men, there might have been selected some student of economics, some professor from one of our numerous universities, a man trained in economic questions of this kind.
The hon. member for Antigonish suggests that I eulogized the United Mine Worker's of America. He is absolutely mis-

taken there. I have not uttered a syllable In this House at any time since I became a member, eulogistic or derogatory of the JJnited Mine Workers' of America^ or any other labour organization of this Dominion.
.1 have said, and I say it again, that when it is conceded to men that they have the fight to belong to a labour organization, they should be permitted to belong to the .organization of their choice, whether it be in affiliation with organizations of another nation, or wholly contained within our own province and country. In order to relieve the hon. member's mind of the idea that perhaps I might be receiving a retainer-I ,do not know what the custom is on the other side-I can assure the hon. member .that I have received no retainer to promote the interests of any labour organization in this House. During the summer of 1909, or, to be accurate, from 19th of July .to the 19th of November, I was solicitor under contract to the United Mine Workers' .of America and acted as their solicitor, afterwards being specially retained in some cases in my own county. That is my whole connection with them, and I have had nothing to do with them, or any other labour organization, either in a professional or any other manner, from that time up to .the present. I have not even had correspondence with them, except that their officers have sent me petitions to be presented asking for the repeal of the Industrial Investigations Act. I am surprised that the hon. member for Antigonish should have suspected that the character of his distinguished friend in Antigonish was so easily susceptible to attack. I am sure that he will read ' Hansard ' in vain for' language of mine that will bear any construction reflecting upon the honour, dignity, or character of the Hon. Justice Mc-Gillivray, for whom I entertain as high a regard in his judicial capacity as the hon. member for Antigonish.

I do not wish to take up time more than is necessary, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) has mentioned as the employees have, but the government, and if I understood the force of his remarks, he would have the country believe that, in some way, due discretion had not been exercised by the government in the choice. I would like to point out to my hon. friend the circumstances under which the choice was made in each instance. In the first place, the companies have the opportunity to name a member of the board, as the employees have, but the government's opportunity to make the appointment does not come until the company has either refused to name a man or has nominated some one whom it is impassible to appoint. This afternoon, in the House, the hon. gentleman asked me if I had observed the petition from the miners of Mr. MADDIN.
Port Morien with regard to the member of the board named by the company.
I mentioned to him that I had refused to appoint the nominee of the company because I had understood he had direct interest or was a shareholder in the concern affected. I then named a member because they refused to name any other member of the board. I named the mayor of Sydney Mines, believing him to be a person who would act fairly on behalf of the company. My hon. friend will say he is a government appointee. But it was not due to any desire on the part of the government that the appointment was made, but because one of the parties failed to name a representative that could be accepted. In selecting a man where either of the parties refuse to name one, my hon. friend will see that our only desire can be to select an impartial man who would be as far as possible acceptable to the interest concerned. If it is the men who have refused to nominate, then some one acceptable to the men should be appointed. I think in some cases the men did refuse to nominate, and in those cases I nominated a man who, I thought would be acceptable to them, and at the same time would give confidence to the community in general. As to the appointment of the chairman, the remaining member of the board, the two parties selected have in the first instance an opportunity to agree upon the chairman; the government has nothing to say in the matter unless they fail to agree, and then we have to appoint the chairman. The idea always is to get some person who, there is reason to believe, will act with strict regard to the justice of the situation. In the province of Nova Scotia I was aware of the fact that the struggle was largely a union struggle, that there was hardly an employer in the mining district of the province who had not taken sides one way or the other, and there was hardly a representative of labour whose views on the question involved were not already known. Therefore, in choosing a chairman, I sought to find some impartial person, and made selections from members of the judiciary, believing they would have no personal ends to serve. I share my hon. friend's admiration for Professor Shortt, and would have appointed him on one or two of these boards if he had been available. But he had already been appointed as chairman of the Civil Service Commission, and for that reason he was not selected. As to the question of legislation compelling recognition of the unions, if the hon. gentleman has any legislation which he would like the government to consider and will submit it, it will be considered. But I would point out that in the province of Nova Scotia at the present time one of the features to be con-

sidered is the fact that you have two unions that are seeking recognition, and that is the main difficulty in Nova Scotia at the present time. There are the United Mine Workers' Association asking the employers to recognize them, and the Provincial Worker's Association asking the employers to recognize them. There you have two labour organizations, each seeking to be recognized by one employer.
That is not so in Spring-hill.

No, but it is in the other two cases. Any law enacted would have to be applicable to all cases, and I cannot think of any law that I could recommend to this House which would meet a situation of that kind, and compel an employer to recognize one union as against another union which is also asking for recognition.
What objection could there be to legislation which would compel an employer to recognize any union to which his men belonged? Supposing there were ten unions.

It depends upon what the hon. gentleman means by recognition. There are different degrees of recognition, one might involve a contract with the union, and one might not involve a contract. If what my hon. friend means is allowing an employee the right to belong to any organization -which he chooses, I think that is a liberty which every man should have. On the same ground I hold the view that an employer should be free to say whom he shall employ, that is a matter of individual liberty. If you concede to the one the right to belong to any organization he chooses, you cannot take away from the other the right to employ whoever he pleases.

What would the minister say where there are two organizations? In the county of Cape Breton a large majority of the men, four-fifths of the men, I believe, belong to the United Mine Workers' Association. Why should they not be recognized as well as the other fifth? Is it not reasonable that the great majority of the working men who belong to the United Mine Workers' Association should be recognized by the employer?

The membership may be divided, as my hon. friend has indicated. But a couple of years ago I think the large majority belonged to the Provincial Workingmen's Association. The position may have changed since then, and it may change again. I don't see that it is going to be possible on the ground of mere numbers to lay down a general rule that is going to be applicable to all cases. I take the same view with regard to membership in labour organizations that I take with
regard to membership in any other organizaation. A man has a right to belong to the Conservative party, a man has a right to belong to the Presbyterian church, and he has the same right to belong to a trades union. But I do not think we can force an employer to employ only Presbyterians, or Conservatives, or trade unionists.
But does not the minister think that minorities have a right to be recognized as well as majorities? The Conservatives are a minority in this House, but does he not think they should be recognized?

I have regard for minorities as well as for majorities. The other evening, in the course of the debate, my hon. friend mentioned that when Mr. Acland', the deputy minister, visited Sydney in September, 1909, to inquire into the conditions of the coal-fields there, Mr. Acland did not go to call upon him, and in fact that he only saw him as he was about to leave South Sydney for North Sydney. Mr. Acland was not here at the time and, of course, I could not reply. But, I may say, in justice to any officer of the government who is not in a position to put his own case before the House when a statement has been made against him, that it is only proper that I should state the circumstance myself. I know that my hon. friend would be the first who would wish that this should be done. Mr. Acland has given me a memorandum on the point and 1 will just read his own statement as I asked him to make it:
I spent from Wednesday, September 1, to Monday, September 6, in Sydney and vicinity. This period included one Sunday and one holiday (Labour Day). I called at Mr. Mad-din's law office in Sydney on two occasions and left an official card. The dates of these calls were Friday, September 3, and Saturday, September 4. On each occasion I was told that Mr. Maddin was at court. My investigations compelled me to be principally out of Sydney or I should doubtless have called more often. I did not learn until later that the court that Mr. Maddin had been attending was at Glace Bay. On Monday, September 6, the courts and offices being closed (it being Labour Day), I hoped to find Mr. Mad-din at his house, and called there at 9.30 a.m., but Mr. Maddin having no telephone at his house I was unable to make an engagement. I was again unsuccessful, Mr. Maddin having left for a picnic at Port Morien; I again left my card with the message that if Mr. Maddin would telephone me at the Sydney hotel I would come out to see him at such time as he named. Mr. Maddin kindly came in the evening to the Sydney hotel, instead of making an engagement, and spent an hour in my room discussing thei situation. Mr. Maddin falls into a slight error in stating that. I was anxious to leave to go to North Sydney to see the representative of the north riding. I had, when I met

Mr. Maddin, only just returned from North Sydney and I had reserved the evening in the hope of meeting Mr. Maddin. My memory and my notes on the subject are clear. I think I understand how Mr. Maddin's error occurred. Nine months later, in June, 1910, I was again in Sydney and vicinity for the purpose of making some inquiries into matters relating particularly to North Sydney. On this occasion I met Mr. Maddin by accident just as I was about ti catch the hoot to North Sydney and I was pleased again to have the opportunity of diseas ing matters with him. I do not remember mentioning the name [DOT] of the member for north riding or stating that it was my intention to s'e him, but it was naturally my intention to speak with him on the subject of my, investigation, should I chance to find him.
I think my hon.. friend will desire that this statement should go on record because it is an explanation which I feel sure that he will be the first to accept.

I have not the slightest objection to its going on record. I could not prevent it from going on record when it is read in the House even if I wished to. The deputy minister says that when he called at my office on Friday and Saturday and left his official card there he got the reply that I was at court but did not know until Monday that I had been attending the court at Glace Bay. He knew I was solicitor for the men and he would naturally infer that I was at Glace Bay. As a matter of fact, I live fully a mile by the car-track from my office in the direction of Glace Bay, and I had my mail brought to my house every morning. A note would have found me, and a card left at my office; would not. I was not going to my office during that time. On the Monday evening, after coming in from the picnic, I went down to see the deputy minister and my recollection is, as I expressed it here two weeks ago to-night, that he said he was going over to see Mr. McKenzie. I have my diary on the matter, not in Ottawa but at home, and I have a memo of the date upon which I met him, and of what took place between us. I had no desire to place Mr. Acland in a false light or misrepresent him. But, it was a very simple matter to have found out from the officers of the United Mine Workers', whom I presume he would see on the Friday or _ Saturday if he went down there to inquire as between the contending parties, exactly where I was because I left every morning at eight o'clock, sometimes at seven, went out to Glace Bay and returned in the evening, sometimes 'at six o'clock and sometimes not till later. I submit that the mere leaving of a card at my office, even although it bore the name and designation of the deputy minister, was not what I would call a very sincere effort to come in contact with me. My stenographer could have told him what court I was engaged Mr. KING.
in, and at what point. He shouid have been able to infer that my duties were in Glace Bay and not Sydney, knowing that I was the solicitor of the men. However, it may be that he did not know that. If he did not know that I was the solicitor of the men then I submit that his conduct in that regard is not open to the same criticism. nowever, I am very glad that he has this explanation to make, and I only, regret that he has not some further explanation to make with regard to where he got his information that the strike was a political one, and had its origin in my runqing against John Moffatt for grand secretary, which took place seven years before the strike.
Combines Investigation Act, $'.0 000
Would the minister tell us if he has had any investigation of combines, and if so, what has been the result?

Up to the present time there have been no investigations of combines under this Act. One application is pending before Judge Cannon of the Superior Court of Quebec on behalf of certain parties who have asked for an investigation into an alleged combine known as the United Shoe Machinery Company. I understand that Judge Cannon will give his finding tomorrow as to whether or not he shall order an investigation in that case. There have been a good many inquiries received by the department for copies of this Act and for the forms which have been drafted under it. I think that the purpose of the Act has been served in part owing to the simple fact of its being on the statute-book because parties know it is there, and they have been more guarded in their actions.
Post Office Department, salaries, $561,080.
There is an increase of $12,320, composed of statutory increases, as follows: 16 of $100 each, 224 of $50 each, 3 of $30 each, and one of $2.
When does the annual postal guide come out?

If the hon. gentleman will send me his requisition I will be glad to send him any number that he requires.
Contingencies, $64,800.
Could the minister give any information with respect to the newspaper item about a new issue of stamps?

We intend to issue a new issue of stamps before the coronation, with the head of His Majesty King George V. We are in correspondence with the High Commissioner, Lord Strathcona, and I expect within a few weeks to have a copy of that stamp to lay before the House.
I wish to ask a few questions with regard to the salaries of inspectors and railway mail clerks.

I suppose . my hon. friend has in mind the proposed increase in salary to the mail clerks. That will come later on. I received a delegation of railway mail clerks the other day, and am to give the railway mail clerks the increase to which they are entitled.
About what would the increase be?

I do not think I would be justified in saying in advance what the increase will be. The deputy minister and I have made up our minds, but the matter has to go before Council. The House will not be disappointed in the measure. I personally intend to give them a substantial increase.
Does it cover all the railway mail clerks?
Yes.
I hope the minister will be liberal in this. I find some first-class railway mail clerks drawing no higher salaries than some messengers in Ottawa.

There are two classes of railway mail clerks. We have some who have not passed the examinations required by the Post Office Act, and, of course, they must pass that examination before being entitled to the railway mileage. It is difficult with the increase of mail matter and of the railway mail service to ask from any applicant that he should pass his examination. Generally they are employed for a probationary period, and then after they have passed their examination they are entitled to their mileage. The mileage differs according to the service to which they are attached. For instance, a railway mail clerk having a service between Ottawa and Montreal would receive less than one who runs between Ottawa and Toronto, or London. Wo generally give the longest runs to the older mail clerks as they get the larger mileage. Of course, there is a grade to which they are entitled according to the length of service they have had in the department.
I wish to ask about the salaries of rural postmasters.

I had the pleasure of increasing their salaries two or three years ago. My hon. friend knows that some years ago the rural postmasters received only a pittance, $12 a year was the minimum. Of course, there is always a minimum and a salary, according to the revenue of each office. Sir William Muloclc increased that salary from $12 to $25, and I increased it
lo $35. I have had representations for a further increase, and it is under consideration. I cannot say at present if their request will be favourably received, but it is under consideration.

While I have no fault to find with the salaries of any servants here in the House, and I think some of them are not receiving enough, there is no employee in any department of the government as badly paid as rural postmasters. You have a daily mail for 300 days in the year, and they get $35. The government of a country like Canada should not ask any one to keep open house for 300 days in the year for $35, or possibly with a iarger revenue, $60. They should get fair play with the rest of the employers of the Dominion of Canada. I think they have been imposed on in the past, and if they do not take the amount offered in many cases the post office is taken away. In my county our post office was closed up for a day, and it was almost impossible to get any one to take it. We offered $35 and $145 for carrying a daily mail 9 miles, or 50 cents a trip.

Of course, my hon. friend is aware that the mail contracts are all made under contract and by tender, and I am bound by the Post Office Act to give them to the lowest tenderer. Under $200 I am, of course, at liberty to increase the amount, according to the increase of mail matter and to the cost of living. In the last two or three years I have taken it on myself, after investigation by the inspectors, to sometimes increase the mail contracts. But when it is beyond $200 I must call for tenders. As regards the pay of rural postmasters, when I say that the matter is under serious consideration by the department at present, it is no vain word, for it is being seriously considered.

The case I mention was not really a contract. We asked for a daily mail service, and we were refused unless we got the mail carried for $145. We succeeded in getting a man to keep the post office for $35, and carry the mail for $145. But we think it is hardly fair to ask any man to carry the mail nine miles and make 300 trips a year for $145. I hope the minister can see his way clear to give the postmasters in the rural parts of the Dominion a substantial increase in their allowances.
I would ask my hon. friend to give me in writing the facts he has stated, and I will certainly take a favourable view of the matter.
I understand that in regard to all the items passed to-night, the Postmaster General will allow them to be discussed at a future time, when his estimates come up again.

I told my hon. friend this afternoon that when postal matters come before the House, it is understood that any question may be brought up concerning post office matters, and I shall be only too pleased to answer them.

There is an item here of $50 for inspecting letter carriers' boots. How are the contracts let for the manufacture of these boots? Are they all made at one place for the whole Dominion, or at different places ?
They are made at different places. We have contractors in all the large cities.
What is the name of the contractor in Toronto ?
I do not remember at present.

The reason I have brought this matter up is, that I know a very good man in Toronto, who has well-equipped establishment for making these boots and who would be veTy pleased to have the contract, and would give good satisfaction.
Tell him to send his application to the department.
What has the minister to say with regard to doing something for the family of R. C. Curren, a railway mail clerk in the Owen Sound district, I believe, who was killed while on service Y

The case is under the consideration of the department. Of course, the family of a railway mail clerk has always a recourse against the railway company. The department is not necessarily responsible in the case oi an accident. Each case is considered by the department, and if it is thought that a compassionate allowance should be given, it is provided for in the estimates and voted by parliament. But we cannot lay it down as a general policy that in every case there will be a compassionate allowance. In any case, there is no recourse in law against the department. It is only a matter of equity, and in such a case, the House may be satisfied that I will do my duty.

When Sir William Mulock was Postmaster General, in 1903, on the 29th of June, he made this statement in the House: I
I have been for a long time contemplating some provision by which the government should decree by statute the payment of a bonus, or a compassionate allowance to the family of a railway mail clerk losing his life in the service, or to himself in case of accident. I am not aware that parliament has ever paid a compassionate allowance to the family of a railway mail clerk who has lost Mr. ARMSTRONG.
his life in the service, until the present government invited parliament to do so, when parliament unanimously agreed to the proposition. It has been our policy ever since coming into power to give a compassionate allowance of $2,000, a fixed sum, to the dependents of a railway mail clerk who has lost his life in the service. But we have not deemed it wise to put that policy into the Act of parliament.
He continued to emphasize that position found a case such as I understand that of the late Mr. Curran, he would grant that amount of money without hesitation. I would also call to the attention of 'the hon. minister another case. Of course he is well aware of the death of the late Mr. Todd, of London district, who lost his life between Goderich and Buffalo. I hope the minister will deal with that case within reasonable time, and in the same spirit as that in .which Sir William Mulock said he dealt with similar cases.

I have no objection to following the policy laid down by Sir William Mulock, but of course my hon. friend will understand that when, as in the case of Mr. Curran, his widow, as I am informed, received from the railway company or the insurance company some $3,000 or $4,000 or $5,000, the urgency is not so great. Each case is examined and dealt with on its own merits.

In the case of Mr. Tye who lost his life between Goderich and Buffalo, I do not see how you could make the railway responsible unless it was held liable for the accident. If not held liable by the coroner's jury, damages could not be recovered from it. There should be some provision to meet a case of that kind.
The department will presently take that matter up. We always take a humane view of these cases.

I hope the hon. minister will also take into consideration the mail clerks in the post office. In the city of London, their work has been doubled. There the mails are transferred north and south and east and west, and the work of the clerks is very heavy. These clerks have not had the increases to which they are entitled, and have been given those in Ottawa. I might remind the minister that if prices have advanced in Ottawa they have also advanced in London. These men have to dress their families and live respectably, and some of them have very low salaries, not larger than those of messengers in the departments at Ottawa.

I would like to ask if it is the intention of the government to bring in this session a superannuation Act for the benefit of the civil service, such as mail clerks, letter carriers, railway mail clerks and the outside service.

That is a question of policy for the government to determine, and on which I could not pronounce at this moment. Superannuation was abolished some years ago, and I have not heard of its being revived, although, I may say, that had I been in the government at that time I might not have supported any such policy. But we are seriously considering the advisability of giving the railway mail clerks and all such employees, a relief, and before the session is through, I hope I shall be able to satisfy my hon. .friend. My hon. friend has been very insistent on this point. He has frequently asked that the department should do a little better for the railway mail clerks, and I must congratulate him on the pertinacity on their behalf.
Is there any provision in the estimates for an increase?
It would be later on. On account of the Post Office Act I would have to introduce it by resolution.

As the hon. minister is contemplating some, ameiid-ments to the Post Office Act, I would like to call his attention to the situation of men who entered the railway mail service before they were 30 years of age. Under the law, unless they pass an examination before reaching that age, they cannot be permanently employed. I have a couple of cases in my mind of considerable hardship. It is rather unfortunate that men perfectly eligible to enter the service and who did enter it at an age somewhat less than thirty, and who for some reason were prevented from passing the examination until they had passed that age, are now not allowed to pass it and cannot be put on the permanent list. It seems to me that there ought to be an amendment to the law which would enable employees who have passed that age, but who are able to pass the- examination, to be allowed to do so and be made permanent. I would ask the hon. minister if he intends submitting any amendment to that effect.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman, but I would add that there are some men in the service, perfectly competent, who, perhaps, will never be able to pass the examination. A man may pass the examination and yet not be competent for the position of railway mail clerk, because that position demands certain qualities of nerve and physique which every one does not possess. A man might not be able to pass a technical examination and yet be a very competent mail clerk and a very competent man on the train. I know of one case where a most excellent mail clerk tried on two or three different occasions to pass. I do not know whether he succeeded in passing in his last attempt,
but I do know that he is a very competent man, and I think there should be some provision for keeping such men in the service, but when taking on new men it might be well to have them undergo an examination.

This question of examination for the railway mail clerks has many difficulties, not only in the east, but especially in the west. It is difficult to get proper men to act as railway mail clerks wdio can pass this examination. This is so much the case that nearly 25 per cent of our railway mail employees are engaged as labourers. Until recently I could not pay these more than $1.50 per day, and yet they are, as a rule, very excellent railway mail clerks.	They could
not, however, pass an examination, and consequently they had .to be employed as labourers. Lately, however, I brought the matter up before the Council, and Council decided that after six months, if these men gave satisfaction I might pay them $2 per day. My view is that wm should make those examinations more pertinent to the work rather than covering the field of knowledge that is at present required.

Does not the minister think that the examination that has to be passed by the clerks in post offices, is a proper one for the railway mail clerks to pass? Does not he think that a railway mail clerk should be as well qualified as a postal clerk ?

The clerk in a city post office has to do a certain class of work and that alone. But the railway mail clerk is, as has been said, ' a postmaster on wheels.' He has to command all the different branches of knowledge required of the postmaster of a large post office. Therefore, he must be better equipped mentally than the man who is merely given a certain piece of work to do during the day. Besides, more regard should be had for the railway mail clerk, who, as stated by my hon. friend a moment ago, has to travel, with all that that implies of nervous strain and danger to health and absence from home, thah to one who serves in the city post office from about eight in the morning to about four or five in the afternoon. I take all that into consideration, and I intend to see that justice is rendered to whomsoever justice is due.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, for I think he is on the right track to do something for the railway mail clerks. I have heard it said that the railway mail clerk was only a stamper and sorter, but have always believed with regard to them, 'what the minister has just stated.
Is it the intention of the minister to place the railway mail service under the Civil Service Commission ?
I hope it is not the intention of the minister to do anything of the kind.
The minister is surely capable of answering the question.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) may think I am purporting to answer the question, but that is not the case. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman wishes to place these officers under the Civil Service Commission or-not, but I do not think it should be done. The hon. member for East Toronto, has told us why. The case of the railway mail clerks 13 a special one, and ought to be dealt with specially. I do not think the law, as it stands to-day, permits of due recognition of the special conditions under which the railway mail clerks serve. If they were put under the hard and fast rules of the Civil Service Commission, it would be still more difficult to recognize their special conditions. I venture to interrupt my hon. friend to say that I hope that the minister entertains no such view.
It is quite out of the ordinary to see a member butt in and answer for the minister.
I did not pretend to answer; the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong), knows that.
The Postmaster General is capable of answering without assistance. I think the question is a fair one, and one that I am justified in asking.

There was a time-to use the language quoted by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), the other day, in my green -and salad days- when I did hope that we could put all the outside service under the Civil Service Act. That was my view two years ago, and even last year. But the more I go into the post office work, and the more I come in contact with the outside service, and the more I see of the working of the new Civil Service Act, the more I am convinced that the railway mail clerks especially, could not be brought under the Civil Service Act. It is too exacting a law. I may tell the House very candidly that it is difficult for the department at Ottawa, even with the university men, who pass very brilliant examinations, before Messrs. Shortt and Laro-chelle, to get the practical men we want. Of course, after a while, the university men, the young students, become quite able to perform the work. But in the case of a service like the railway mail service, it would be impossible to get the work done Mr. RUSSELL.
if _we had to apply to the Civil Service Commission at Ottawa, -and employ men only as they -could send them to us. As to the railway mail service, you have no idea, Mr. Chairman, of the difficulty we have, especially in the west, to get the proper men. The young men will not take the office of railway mail clerk. They object to it, and ask for pay which w'e cannot -afford to give and to which they are not entitled. The railway development of the country is so great, and the service is increasing so rapidly and its extension is so large that it would be impossible for us to depend upon -a supply -of railway mail clerks through the Civil Service Commission. I had the idea a year or two ago that it could be done, but I must recant and say that the railway mail service, in my judgment, m-ust always remain an outside service. As regards the large city post offices like Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, Toronto, Winnipeg, the supply of officers needed during the rush seasons, is also a difficult matter. 1 am studying that point. My views are shared by the highest officers of my department. But, in my judgment, we should try to bring these officers under the Civil Service Commission, I hope to be able to do it some day, but it is a question to be carefully studied, before deciding the point.

The minister said something a short time ago about the labourers in the city post offices. Does not he -think it beneath his dignity to employ a lot of clerks and call them labourers for the sole purpose of evading the provisions of the Act ? Does he not think it would be better to amend the Act in such a way as to allow him -to employ these people under their proper title as clerks ? The matter is referred to in the Auditor General's Report.
Would they not come under the head of porters ?

Some do; for instance, those who carry on the exchange of mails at Toronto, Montreal and other large places. There are porters-regularly empoyees. But others who have some qualifications, but are not ready to take the examination, are needed in the rush seasons in the large post offices. They are appointed as labourers. I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor, New Westminster) that those who want to

come in are not ashamed to come in under the title of ' labourers ' provided they get a suitable salary.

1 think it was beneath the dignity of a minister of the Crown to employ a lot of persons in an occupation where he was not authorized by law to appoint them, and to beat the devil around the bush by calling them labourers. That was the dignity I referred to.

If the hon. gentleman reads the correspondence exchanged between the Auditor General and my department, he will find that we had not recourse to that class of men in order to carry out the work of the department, otherwise it could not be carried out. At the Christmas season and at Easter, in all the large cities, we had to take a certain number of men on temporarily and pay them as labourers. I explained that to the Auditor General. It has been the custom for many years.

-The minister suggested that there was a good deal of difficulty in getting the right class of labour for the various branches of his department. 1 did not understand whether it was owing to the defective education supplied by our universities that he was getting an inferior class of men, or whether it was that the men were not sufficiently paid. 1 believe throughout my hon. friend's department the men are not paid in proportion to their responsibility. It is my opinion that of all the departments in the government the last one that can be justified in showing a surplus is the Rost Office Department. It is a matter of such tremendous utility and importance to the whole people of the country, that too much attention cannot be paid to the officers who administer it. He said he had difficulty in getting adequate and capable men in the west for railway clerks and other branches of his department. The further west he goes the higher wages he will have to pay all round, and unless you pay adequate remuneration you are not likely to get the class of men that you need. The Postmaster General cannot afford to be niggardly in that respect. I have in my hand a request that meets with a good deal of sympathy from me, it is a memorial signed, I believe, by some 6,000 postmasters. Here are the requests they make:
1.	An increase in salary to meet the sharp advance in the cost of living.
2.	An increase in the rent allowance, and the placing of it on the straight percentage basis.
3.	Necessary supplies, such as twine, ink, pens, pencils, &c., to be furnished by the department.
Now, these are all reasonable requests, especially the last one.
4.	The postmasters to be given greater protection in the purchase of good equipment for offices.
5.	That offices be classified, and a system of promotion (optional for a time) be established, with a view to promoting greater efficiency and permanency.
I think the postmasters deserve our sympathy in that request. There is no doubt that greater efficiency and permanency would be promoted by placing the postmasters on a civil service basis. The day has come for the government to take a step forward in that direction.
6.	Better newspaper labelling, with a view to greater despatch and accuracy.
7.	Full recognition of the association by the government, that postmasters may establish a system of post relief and make suggestions from time to time.
8.	That a copy of the Postmaster General's report be sent to each accounting office.
I am sure the Postmaster General will see the reasonableness of a request like that. I am getting requests continually from postmasters for a copy of the Postmaster General's Report, and I have no doubt the postmasters would read it with more interest than the members of this House read it.
9.	That where safes are advisable, they be furnished by the department.
10.	Throwing the civil service insurance open to postmasters.
11.	A more adequate night service.
At this hour of the night I do not propose to discuss the merits of each one of these claims, but I feel sure they will all appeal to the Postmaster General's sense of justice. They all seem entirely reasonable. He must remember that upon this class of men great responsibilities are thrown, they are men from whom every one of us requires the very full performance of small duties as well as great. 1 think a generous recognition should be given to this class of the public service.
This petition has already been forwarded to me by the Postmaster's Association, and by several members of the House. It is under consideration by the department.
Favourable?

I would not say favourable consideration for each particular item, but it is being considered very seriously by the department. We have always taken their part in the past, at least I take credit for doing so. If they have had an increase in their salary they owe it to me. I am glad my hon. friend has made these remarks as an adjunct to the petition presented by the Postmasters' Association.

I would like to endorse what my hon. friend

has said in favour of that petition. I would also take this occasion of asking the minister whether there is anything in this item for a post office at Central Park, as to which we had some conversation last year. It is near New Westminster.
I have not got the papers before me. Is the condition the same as it was last year?
I heard that the minister's deputy had visited the locality this year and had given the people some encouragement.

If my deputy has given the Central Park people some encouragement, my hon. friend may rest assured that the post office will be established, because he generally goes one better than the Postmaster General. He has been there to see what the requirements are. I think he found great improvement in that particular section of British Columbia ; he found a new Vancouver, a new New Westminster and a new Victoria. He was much surprised to see the increased population and business in those cities. He spent a month there at the request of the Prime Minister, who took my place during my absence.

If the minister will refer to his deputy he will find that the representations I made last year as to Central park were fully borne out. The minister will remember that the office was closed, and another office bearing the same name was established about a mile away. We had a long conversation about it last year, and the minister promised to give it attention.
I will have a report upon it.

I would like to point out to the minister that while the boundaries of Vancouver city have very recently been extended so as to come very close to where the post office at Central park was, that would not be an adequate reason for not reopening that office because, following on the extension of the Vancouver boundaries that far, there has been opened up another district which will add as much on the east of that old Central Park post office as will be taken off in the west for inclusion in the Vancouver service.
Is there a street railway service there?

There is the Interurban tram which passes through Central park from Vancouver to New Westminster. But the district is settling very fast, and although half of the persons who petitioned the department have now been included in Vancouver and will Mr. TAYLOR (New Westminster!.
get the city service there will, in a few months, be some other places contiguous to Central Park who will require post office facilities. I would be glad if the minister would inquire into the matter.
I will have to take the case up with my deputy.

I have had some correspondence along the same line as that read by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) and I would heartily agree in the recommendation made by the hon. member that the postmasters in the outside service should be more adequately paid. I think that some more liberal allowance should be made for rent for post offices in smaller towns. I do not know whether an allowance is made or whether the department pays the rent, but I know that in many towns very inferior buildings are used for post office purposes, and that they are not adequate to the proportions and importance of the towns in which they are situated. In many cases very much better post offices could be provided for a very small additional sum. [DOT]

I would like to ask the minister if in all cases every clerk in the outside service is treated equally and equitably with regard to statutory allowances' and things of that kind. I have in mind now, although I have no list with me that we have in the post office in St. John men who have been there a great many years, and I think, are entitled _ to iarger salaries than they are getting. These men are not getting as much as others who have come in and .who occupy what may be called _ inferior positions, certainly junior positions. It is not encouraging to young men to enter the service if they can see inequalities in the treatment of clerks ahead of them which may possibly be due to changes in government but which ought not to occur under any circumstances. The minister was complaining just now of the difficulty of getting suitable men to occupy-positions in the postal service. I "think that probably is one of the reasons why he is not as successful as he ought to be. The men, when they go into the government service, go in with the expectation of being treated equitably. Every one expects to be put on the same footing, and to be treated with the same amount of consideration. If the minister expects, as I have no doubt he wishes, to have a contented and satisfactory service, all the officials in his department ought to be able to feel that they would be treated with the same consideration no matter by whom appointed according to their length of service, and things of that kind. Governments change and even the government of which my hon. friend is such an orna-I ment may some day cross to the_ other side of the House. He would not like to feel

that all those gentlemen whom he appointed might suffer on that account, and I think that every official ought to be equitably treated no matter by whom appointed. 1 think the minister will agree that what 1 am saying is reasonable, and I hope that he will see to it that no injustice may continue to be done as I think injustice is now being done in St. John.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) will draw my attention to any such injustice I will certainly do my best to remedy it, but I may inform my hon. friend that as far as I and the head officers of my department are concerned there is no prejudice whatever concerning matters of this kind. Men come into the department after passing the examination required by the Post Office Act, they enter in a certain * class and then they go up automatically every year provided that the inspector, the' postmaster and the general superintendent agree that the officer has been a faithful' employee. It is not to my knowledge that in the many post offices we have in the country any injustice has been done for really it is a shame to deprive a man of his increase merely for political considerations. My hon. friend knows that I am myself a son of a civil servant and I know how in days gone by we were sometimes sad on account of the poor salary that my father received he being the head of a very large family. He never complained himself, he was treated fairly by the ministers of his department although he was known to be a good Grit himself. I want to see the same fairness shown towards all the emifloyees to-day as the ministers of old extended to my own father. It is not to my knowledge that any man has been deprived of his increase on account of his political proclivities. I can assure my hon. friend that if any case arises where in his judgment, or in the judgment of an employee, an injustice has been done he has only to report the case to me, and I will see that it is dealt with in fairness and equity.
The first time I am down home I will look up this matter and bring it to the notice of the minister.
Does the minister know of a Bill considered in the Senate last year dealing with superannuation, and is there any likelihood it will reach the House this session?	,

I think it was considered by the Senate as an academic proposition. Of course that question would have to be decided by the government. Many wise people think we should return to the superannuation system.

I was glad to hear the minister is increasing the salaries of postal
clerks and railway mail clerks. So many new post offices are being erected by the Public Works Department that the Postmaster General will be relieved of many rental charges and I anticipated that this increase would be made. I would suggest that no clerk in the postal service living in the city should get less than $1,000 a year. The salary of $400 which used to be the minimum was quite insufficient. I believe there is no man in the country who ought to be protected by parliament to the same extent as the civil servant if lie faithfully discharges his duty. I wish to mention the case of a lady in Halifax who was in the service some years ago and then left the service and owing to circumstances over which she had no control returned to it. In the meantime she was deprived of the advantage that would come to her of superannuation, Representations have been made and I hope the case will be favourably considered.
I will take up the case.
We have some cases in Halifax, such as have been referred to by the hon. member for St. John, of men who complain of being in the department many years but who have been caught up to by younger men.
The deputy informs me he has instructed Mr. Ross to prepare a list of the men who have been long in the service in order to review their salaries.

We have also many cases of poorly paid rural postmasters in my district, one Mr. Wesley Crooks, who has been in the postal service for 46 years, who has a daily mail which must have increased gieatly in that time, and is now getting what he commenced with. $30 a year and nothing for rent. I trust the Postmaster General will be particularly kind to that gentleman. It is so long since he entered the service that I forget the politics of the government in power at that time. I know this man very well, and I think he has been postmaster for some 46 years, which would indicate that he is pretty well up in years. His name is Crooks, and the name of the place is Peggy's Cove. He is a very active and capable man, and I think is entitled to some reasonable increase.
I will look into the matter.

I wish to ask that a small post office in the province of Saskatchewan called Lajord should be made an accounting post office. It has considerable revenue and it would be a great convenience to the town and district.
I will make a note of it, and if it is possible it will be done.
Does the same schedule of salaries for postmasters prevail in the east as in the west?
There is a special allowance to the west.

Some post offices in the east have been closed, while in the west new post offices are being opened. Some have been closed in my own riding, though they have been open for over 40 years. One has been closed at New Harmony, the reason given being that the revenue was very small. But there are as many people in the settlement as there were when the office was opened. The reason the revenue is so small is that it has only a tri-weekly service, while the next post office, 3 or 4i miles distant, has a daily service, and the people go there for their mail, leaving the other office almost forsaken.
I will take a note of it.

Another matter. There is a string of nine post offices near Souris, in almost a continuous chain. One carrier carries the mail to all of them, but three or four have a daily mail service, while - the others have only a tri-weekly service.
I am having a report on that very matter at present from the deputy, and as soon as I get it I will send a copy of it to my hon. friend.
Has the Postmaster General done anything with regard to a free mail delivery in North Toronto?
I am going to Toronto on Monday, and that is one of the matters which I am to discuss with Mr. Ross.
What about the post office at Mimico Beach, -which I asked for last year?
I will get the papers.

I observe by the Postmaster General's Report this year that he is claiming a surplus of $743,210.25 on the year's business. I do not suppose that any person except the Postmaster General entertains the idea that the Post Office Department should be a money-making department, and therefore, in view of the very substantial surplus which the Postmaster General has, I do not think I need be at all diffident in pressing this matter upon his attention. There is a request from the residents of Meteghan Centre, in Digby, This village is situated midway between Meteghan and Meteghan River. " The mail carrier in travelling from Meteghan station passes through Meteghan River and so on to Meteghan and on the way, necessarily passes through the village of Meteghan Centre. There is no post office at Meteghan Centre, at present, but there are Mr. LEMIEUX.
some 50 families resident there, besides a store and milling concern, and the business is increasing. The people therefore feel greatly the need of a post office. When I presented their petition for one, the answer which the department gave me was that inasmuch as there was a post office at Meteghan and one at Meteghan River, and as these were not very far from Meteghan Centre, there did not appear to be any great necessity of a post office at Meteghan Centre. The cost, however, of opening an office would not be very great. I think that the minimum salary which the Postmaster General pays for small offices is $35, and that would be what he would have to pay there. The transportation of the mails would probably not coist anything, because the mail passes through there now on its way to Meteghan, so that the total cost would be only $35 per year for providing the necessary postal facilities for a very prosperous and thriving village and one which has a bright future. Under the circumstances and considering the substantial surplus which the post office department enjoys, I think , that the request I make is a very reasonable one.
What is the distance between Meteghan Centre and the others.
About two miles each way.

As there is no mail carrier to pay, I think my hon. friend has made out a veTy good case, and if he would send me over the papers, I think I can meet his views.
%
Do I understand the minister to say that he is convinced because if not, I have more facts which I would present and which will make the case still stronger.
My hon. friend says it is two miles from each office.
Approximately. I have travelled the road many times, and that is the distance to the best of my judgment.
It is all right.

I hope the minister will allow us to take up matters pertaining to this item at any future time. I intend to emphasize the necessity of rural free mail delivery and there are others not here, who are prepared to take up the same question.

That question must necessarily come up, because I shall have an announcement to make with regard to it,
Mail service, $1,137,700.

There are some other members who would like to ask questions

with regard to this matter and I think the hon. minister should not proceed any further as it is now past midnight and there are very few in the House.
I have other estimates to bring up and every opportunity will be given to ask questions on anything connected with the mails when they are submitted.
Having passed the first item, I think we have done very well.

I want the whole item of 309 to pass as I require the money, but I give my hon. friend the assurance that if he or any of his friends want to discuss the general item of post offices, there will be no objection whatever, and they will have every opportunity of doing so on other items.
I think the minister is asking something very unreasonable when he asks us to pass the whole of his estimates at this hour of the night.
I have other estimates to bring before the House.

We have had a long day, and the minister brought on his estimates very late. He can hardly expect us to pass this whole item covering an expenditure of over $8,000,000 with so few members here. I myself have a good many questions to ask, and I do not think that I should be forced to enter into a discussion at this late hour. We have had a very long day as it is.

I am in the hands of the House, but I understood that I had made an arrangement with the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), and until my friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) made an objection, there was no disposition to prevent this item going through.

I did not understand that all these estimates were to go through in an hour's time. We have passed some $4,000,000 already, and I think we ought to stop there and give opportunity for further discussion.
Suppose we leave ' miscellaneous ' and carry the mail service.
These different estimates are all part of the one item, and you cannot hold over an item in part and pass it in part.
You can leave the last item.
The Postmaster General will understand that all these estimates are part of the one item 309, and either the' whole of item 309 stands or it passes. I appeal to the chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I, of course, am only too willing to respect any arrangement that both sides may come to; but if objection be raised, there are certain rules of procedure which I may be compelled to enforce.
All the four services are under the one item, and it can be of no use to the Postmaster general to pass three-quarters of them and not the other quarter.

I do not wish to insist more that I should. But I thought we had discussed very fully every item. However, at the special request of my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) I waive any objection I might have.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Mr. Lemieux, House adjourned at 12.20 a.m., Saturday.

Monday, February 27, 1911.
